title: Economic growth
overview: Economic growth is an increase in the real output of goods and services in an economy over time, normally measured by the percentage change in real GDP. This topic is about how growth is measured (real vs nominal, totals vs per capita, GDP vs GNI), how to compare countries fairly using purchasing power parities, and how far GDP really captures living standards compared with measures of national happiness and well-being. Calculation questions on real values and per capita figures appear regularly in Section A, and 'how useful is GDP?' evaluation is a staple of data-response questions.
objectives: Define economic growth and GDP and explain the difference between real and nominal values.
Calculate real GDP from nominal GDP and a price index, real growth rates and GDP per capita.
Distinguish GDP from GNI and explain when the difference matters.
Explain why purchasing power parities are used to compare GDP between countries and calculate a PPP-adjusted figure.
Evaluate the use of GDP as a measure of living standards, including the limitations of GDP and the role of national happiness (well-being) measures.

sections.heading: What economic growth is and how GDP is measured
sections.body:
**Gross domestic product (GDP)** is the total value of goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period, usually a quarter or a year. **Economic growth** is an increase in real GDP over time. In the UK the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes a monthly GDP estimate and quarterly estimates, which are revised several times as more data arrive.

GDP can be measured in three ways, which in principle give the same answer because one person's spending is another person's income and every pound of spending buys some output:
- **Output method**: add up the value added at each stage of production across all industries (counting only value added avoids double counting of intermediate goods).
- **Income method**: add up all factor incomes earned in production: wages, profits, rent and interest.
- **Expenditure method**: add up spending on final output: C + I + G + (X - M).

Distinguish two ideas that students often merge:
- **Actual growth** is the measured rise in real GDP, which can come from using idle resources (moving towards the PPF) as well as from more capacity.
- **Potential growth** is an increase in the productive capacity of the economy (an outward shift of the PPF or a rightward shift of LRAS), caused by more or better factors of production.

Growth is usually reported as an annual percentage rate or a quarter-on-quarter rate. A widely used (but not official) rule of thumb defines a **recession** as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth. Small changes matter: a trend growth rate of 2.5% doubles real output in about 28 years (the rule of 70: 70 divided by the growth rate), whereas 1% takes about 70 years. This is why the UK's slow growth since the 2008 financial crisis is such a big policy concern.

sections.heading: Real versus nominal GDP
sections.body:
**Nominal GDP** (money GDP, GDP at current prices) values output at the prices of the year in which it was produced. If prices rise, nominal GDP rises even if not a single extra good is produced. **Real GDP** (GDP at constant prices) removes the effect of inflation by valuing output at the prices of a base year, so it measures the change in the volume of output.

To convert nominal to real you divide by a price index. For GDP the correct index is the **GDP deflator**, which covers all domestically produced output, not just the consumer basket used for CPI:

Real GDP = nominal GDP x (price index in base year / price index in current year)

**Worked example.** Nominal GDP is £2,000bn in year 1 (base year, deflator = 100) and £2,140bn in year 2 (deflator = 104).
- Nominal growth = (2,140 - 2,000) / 2,000 x 100 = 7.0%.
- Real GDP in year 2 = 2,140 x 100 / 104 = £2,057.7bn.
- Real growth = (2,057.7 - 2,000) / 2,000 x 100 = 2.9%.

A quick approximation is real growth ≈ nominal growth - inflation (7% - 4% = 3%), but in a calculation question always use the exact method and show the working.

Why it matters: in 2022 UK nominal GDP rose strongly because inflation was around 10%, yet real growth was only a few per cent. A politician quoting nominal figures in a period of high inflation can make the economy look far healthier than it is. The same logic applies to wages: if average pay rises 6% while CPI inflation is 9%, **real wages fall** by roughly 3%, which is what happened to many UK workers in 2022.

sections.heading: Totals, per capita figures and growth rates
sections.body:
Total real GDP tells you the size of an economy; **real GDP per capita** (real GDP divided by population) tells you the average output, and hence average income, per person. For living standards per capita is much more useful, because a bigger population shares the output.

**Worked example.** Real GDP rises from £2,000bn to £2,057.7bn while the population rises from 67.0m to 68.5m.
- Real GDP per capita, year 1 = £2,000bn / 67.0m = £29,851.
- Real GDP per capita, year 2 = £2,057.7bn / 68.5m = £30,039.
- Growth in real GDP per capita = (30,039 - 29,851) / 29,851 x 100 = 0.6%, far less than the 2.9% growth in total real GDP.

This is a live UK issue. In 2023 total real GDP grew only slightly while the population grew rapidly because of high net migration, so real GDP per head fell, often described as a 'per capita recession'. It is perfectly possible for total GDP to rise while the average person is no better off.

Other points to handle carefully:
- A **fall in the growth rate** is not a fall in GDP. If growth slows from 3% to 1%, GDP is still rising, just more slowly. Read data-response tables and charts carefully: is the vertical axis a level or a rate of change?
- Per capita is an **average** and says nothing about distribution. Mean GDP per capita can rise while median household income stagnates if gains go to the top.
- **Index numbers** are often used to show GDP over time (base year = 100). An index of 112 means 12% higher than the base year, but a move from 112 to 118 is a 5.4% rise, not 6%.

sections.heading: GDP and GNI
sections.body:
**Gross national income (GNI)** measures the income earned by a country's residents and firms wherever in the world it is produced. It equals GDP plus net primary income from abroad (income such as profits, dividends, interest and employee pay received from abroad minus the same flows paid to foreigners).

GNI = GDP + income received from abroad - income paid abroad

For most large economies the gap is small, but it can be large where:
- **Foreign multinationals dominate production.** Ireland is the classic case. Large US firms book profits and intellectual property in Ireland, so Irish GDP is inflated by output whose profits flow abroad. Irish GDP was recorded as rising by over 25% in 2015 after a few firms relocated assets, a figure that told you almost nothing about Irish living standards. The Irish authorities now publish a modified measure (GNI*) because GDP is so distorted.
- **Many nationals work abroad and send money home** (remittances). Strictly, remittances are secondary income transfers, so they are added to get gross national disposable income, but the principle is the same: domestic output understates what residents can spend.
- **A country owns large overseas assets.** Countries with big sovereign wealth funds, such as Norway, earn substantial investment income from abroad.

For the UK, net primary income has swung between surplus and deficit over the last two decades, so UK GNI and GDP are close. The examiner wants you to know which measure suits the question: GDP for the level of production and employment at home; GNI for the income available to residents. This links directly to the primary income section of the current account (2.1.4).

sections.heading: Comparing countries: purchasing power parities
sections.body:
To compare GDP between countries you must convert to a common currency, usually US dollars. Using **market exchange rates** is misleading for two reasons: exchange rates are volatile (driven by capital flows and speculation as much as trade), and they do not reflect the fact that non-traded goods and services such as haircuts, housing and public transport are much cheaper in low-income countries.

**Purchasing power parity (PPP)** exchange rates are the rates at which the same basket of goods and services costs the same in each country. GDP converted at PPP compares the actual volume of goods and services each country's income can buy.

**Worked example.** In Zedland (fictional), GDP per capita is 300,000 zeds. The market exchange rate is 60 zeds = $1, giving $5,000 per head. A representative basket costs $100 in the USA and 2,400 zeds in Zedland, so the PPP rate is 24 zeds = $1. GDP per capita at PPP = 300,000 / 24 = $12,500. Zedland's citizens can buy two and a half times more than the market-rate figure suggests.

Key points:
- PPP raises the measured GDP of low and middle-income countries relative to rich ones, because their non-traded services are cheap. India and China look much larger at PPP than at market rates; at PPP China's total GDP has been larger than the USA's for several years.
- PPP figures depend on price surveys (the World Bank's International Comparison Program) and on choosing a representative basket, which is hard when consumption patterns differ sharply.
- The Economist's Big Mac index is a light-hearted version of the same idea, using one product.

sections.heading: How well does GDP measure living standards?
sections.body:
Living standards depend on the material and non-material quality of life. Real GDP per capita at PPP is the most widely used single proxy because it is objective, regularly collected and broadly comparable. But it has significant limitations:
- **The hidden (informal) economy.** Cash-in-hand work and illegal activity are only partially estimated. This matters most in developing economies, where informal work can be a large share of output, so GDP understates living standards there.
- **Unpaid work and household production** such as childcare and caring for elderly relatives is excluded. If a parent goes back to work and pays a childminder, GDP rises even though the same care is being provided.
- **Quality and new products.** GDP struggles with improvements in quality and free digital services: a smartphone today is vastly better than in 2010 at a similar price, and free search and maps add to welfare with little recorded output.
- **Externalities and sustainability.** Pollution, congestion and resource depletion are not subtracted. Clean-up spending after a flood or an oil spill actually adds to GDP.
- **Distribution.** A rise in mean income can coincide with rising inequality and stagnant incomes for most households.
- **Composition of output.** Spending on defence or prisons counts the same as spending on education or health.
- **Leisure and working hours.** If people work longer hours GDP rises, but welfare may not.

None of these mean GDP is useless; they mean it should be interpreted alongside other indicators. Over long periods, rising GDP per capita has been strongly associated with longer life expectancy, better health and more education, which is why it remains central.

sections.heading: National happiness and well-being
sections.body:
Because GDP is only a partial measure, governments increasingly measure **subjective well-being**. Since 2011 the ONS has asked large samples of adults four personal well-being questions, scored 0 to 10: life satisfaction, whether the things they do are worthwhile, how happy they felt yesterday and how anxious they felt yesterday. These sit within a wider set of National Well-being indicators covering health, relationships, environment, education and finance. Bhutan famously uses Gross National Happiness as a guiding objective, and the annual World Happiness Report ranks countries, with Nordic countries such as Finland regularly at the top.

Evidence on the link between income and happiness:
- The **Easterlin paradox**: within a country, richer people report higher happiness than poorer people, but over time, as a country gets richer, average reported happiness rises little. Explanations include **relative income** (people compare themselves with others), **adaptation** (people get used to higher income) and the rising importance of non-material factors once basic needs are met.
- More recent cross-country research finds that life satisfaction does rise with the logarithm of income, so a given percentage rise in income adds similar happiness at all levels. That means an extra £1,000 matters far more to a poor household than a rich one, which supports the view that **diminishing marginal utility of income** links growth, inequality and welfare.
- Happiness is strongly affected by unemployment (beyond the lost income), health, relationships and security. This is a powerful argument for policy to prioritise employment and mental health rather than GDP alone.

Limitations of happiness data: answers are subjective, culturally influenced and sensitive to question order and current events; scores are bounded at 10, so they cannot keep rising as GDP can; and it is hard to design policy directly around them. Composite measures such as the Human Development Index (life expectancy, education and GNI per capita at PPP) are a middle way, covered in 4.3.1.

key_terms.definition: An increase in the real output of goods and services in an economy over time, usually measured as the annual percentage change in real GDP.
The total value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given time period.
GDP measured at current prices, so it includes the effect of inflation as well as changes in the volume of output.
GDP measured at constant (base year) prices, so the effect of inflation is removed and it shows changes in the volume of output.
A price index covering all domestically produced goods and services, used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP.
GDP divided by the population; an average measure of output and income per person.
GDP plus net primary income from abroad: the income earned by a country's residents and firms wherever production takes place.
An exchange rate at which the same basket of goods and services costs the same in two countries; used to compare real living standards across countries.
A period of falling real GDP, commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth.
People's own assessment of their quality of life, such as life satisfaction and happiness, measured through surveys such as the ONS personal well-being questions.
The finding that richer people within a country report greater happiness, but rising national income over time is associated with little rise in average reported happiness.
Economic activity that is not declared to the authorities, such as cash-in-hand work or illegal trade, and so is poorly captured in GDP.

diagrams.title: Nominal and real GDP over time
diagrams.caption: Both series are equal in the base year. Afterwards nominal GDP rises faster because it includes rising prices; the vertical gap is the effect of inflation, and only the real GDP line measures economic growth.

diagrams.title: Actual and potential growth on a PPF
diagrams.caption: Moving from A (unemployed resources) to B on PPF1 is actual growth with no change in capacity. The outward shift from PPF1 to PPF2, caused by more or better factors of production, is potential growth.

formulae.name: Real GDP
formulae.formula: Nominal GDP x (price index in base year / price index in current year)
formulae.example: Nominal GDP £2,140bn, deflator 104 (base 100): real GDP = 2,140 x 100 / 104 = £2,057.7bn.

formulae.name: Growth rate
formulae.formula: (Value this period - value last period) / value last period x 100
formulae.example: Real GDP rises from £2,000bn to £2,057.7bn: growth = 57.7 / 2,000 x 100 = 2.9%.

formulae.name: GDP per capita
formulae.formula: GDP / population

formulae.name: GNI
formulae.formula: GDP + primary income from abroad - primary income paid abroad
formulae.example: GDP £500bn, income received from abroad £30bn, income paid abroad £45bn: GNI = £485bn.

formulae.name: GDP at PPP
formulae.formula: GDP in local currency / PPP exchange rate
formulae.example: 300,000 zeds per head / 24 zeds per $ = $12,500 per head at PPP (vs $5,000 at the market rate of 60 zeds per $).

applications: The UK economy produced roughly £2.8 trillion of output in 2024, but growth since the 2008 financial crisis has averaged well under the roughly 2.5% a year typical before it. With strong population growth from net migration, real GDP per head fell during 2023, a period widely described as a per capita recession, which helps explain why many households felt worse off despite headline GDP not falling much.

UK GDP figures are revised substantially. The UK was initially estimated to have entered a shallow technical recession in the second half of 2023, and the COVID-19 period saw large revisions to growth estimates. Policy makers such as the Bank of England MPC therefore treat first estimates with caution and look at surveys (such as purchasing managers' indices) alongside official data.

Ireland shows why GDP and GNI can diverge: multinational profit-shifting produced recorded GDP growth of over 25% in 2015. The Irish government now uses modified GNI (GNI*) to judge the size of its economy and to set debt and spending ratios.

At market exchange rates the USA is the world's largest economy, but at PPP China has been larger for several years, and India rises to third. Any international comparison in an essay should state which conversion has been used.

The ONS Measuring National Well-being programme shows that UK average life satisfaction fell during the pandemic and anxiety rose, even in periods when GDP was recovering quickly, illustrating that output and well-being can move differently in the short run.
evaluation: It depends on the purpose: real GDP per capita is a good measure of material output and average income, and is closely correlated with health and education over the long run, but it is a poor measure of distribution, sustainability or non-material welfare.

Magnitude matters: for rich countries with small informal sectors, hidden-economy errors are modest; for low-income countries where informal work may be a large share of activity, GDP understates living standards by much more.

Short run vs long run: quarterly GDP is volatile and heavily revised, so judgements about recession or recovery based on one or two quarters are unreliable. Trend growth over a decade is far more meaningful.
Averages hide distribution: mean GDP per capita can rise while median household disposable income stagnates. Combine GDP with Gini coefficients or median income for a fair picture.

Alternative measures have their own weaknesses: happiness scores are subjective, bounded at 10 and culturally biased, and HDI uses arbitrary weights. The best answer is usually a dashboard of indicators rather than a single replacement for GDP.

PPP comparisons are better than market exchange rates for living standards, but rely on infrequent price surveys and a common basket, so small PPP differences between countries should not be over-interpreted.
misconceptions: Confusing a fall in the growth rate with a fall in GDP. If growth falls from 2% to 0.5%, output is still rising. Only negative growth means output is falling.

Using CPI to deflate GDP in an essay without comment. CPI only covers consumer prices; the GDP deflator covers all domestic output, including investment and exports. In exam calculations, use whichever index the question gives you.
Thinking that a rise in nominal GDP means the economy has grown. Without knowing inflation you cannot tell whether output has risen at all.
Assuming GDP per capita tells you what a typical person earns. It is a mean, which is pulled up by very high incomes; the median is usually lower.
Treating GDP and GNI as interchangeable. They differ by net primary income from abroad, which can be very large for countries such as Ireland or Luxembourg.
exam_tips: In calculation questions, state the formula, show each step and give units (£bn, %), and round sensibly (one or two decimal places). Many marks are lost for confusing percentage changes with percentage point changes.
When a data extract gives nominal figures and an inflation rate, examiners often expect you to notice that real growth is much smaller. Use the numbers explicitly to gain application marks.

For evaluation of GDP as a measure of living standards, do not just list limitations. Pick two or three, explain why each matters for the specific country in the extract, and reach a judgement on whether GDP is still the best available single measure.

Synoptic link: growth measures feed into output gaps (2.5.2), the trade cycle (2.5.3) and development measures such as HDI (4.3.1). A 25-mark Paper 2 or 3 essay on growth benefits from this wider context.

model_answer.question: Evaluate whether real GDP per capita is the best measure for comparing living standards between the UK and a low-income country. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Living standards refer to the material and non-material quality of life of a population. Real GDP per capita is total output at constant prices divided by population, so it measures the average volume of goods and services available per person. For international comparisons it is normally converted into US dollars at purchasing power parity, the exchange rate at which a common basket of goods costs the same in each country.

There are strong reasons why real GDP per capita at PPP is the most widely used measure. First, it is objective and collected in a broadly consistent way by national statistics agencies using international accounting standards, so the UK and a low-income country can be compared on a similar basis. Second, using real rather than nominal values removes inflation, which is vital if the low-income country has high inflation; otherwise its nominal income would appear to grow quickly when real output was flat. Third, adjusting at PPP rather than market exchange rates allows for the much lower price of non-traded goods such as housing, food and services in low-income countries. For example, if a low-income country's GDP per head is $2,000 at market rates but its prices are about a third of UK levels, its PPP figure would be around $6,000, giving a far more realistic picture of what people can actually consume. Finally, over the long run higher GDP per capita is strongly correlated with longer life expectancy and more years of schooling, because higher incomes fund healthcare, sanitation and education.

However, there are significant reasons why GDP per capita may mislead in this particular comparison. The informal economy is much larger in many low-income countries, where a significant share of work in agriculture, street trading and domestic service is unrecorded, and subsistence farming produces food that is consumed rather than sold. This means GDP understates living standards in the low-income country more than in the UK, so the gap between them is exaggerated. In addition, GDP per capita is a mean. If income in the low-income country is very unequally distributed, for example because mineral export revenues accrue to a small elite or to foreign multinationals, then average GDP per head could be quite high while most of the population lives in poverty. In that case GNI, which excludes profits paid abroad, plus a distribution measure such as the Gini coefficient would be more informative. GDP also ignores non-material factors: the UK's higher life expectancy, political stability and environmental quality are part of its living standards but only appear indirectly, while long working hours or pollution in a rapidly industrialising economy reduce well-being without reducing GDP.

Alternative measures address some of these weaknesses. The Human Development Index combines life expectancy, education and GNI per capita at PPP, so it captures health and education directly, which matters most at low income levels. Subjective well-being surveys, such as the ONS life satisfaction measure, capture how people feel about their lives, but they are culturally biased and bounded at 10, so they are less useful for comparing countries at very different stages of development.

In conclusion, real GDP per capita at PPP is the best single starting point because it is objective, widely available and closely linked to the resources people have to improve their lives. However, for a comparison between the UK and a low-income country it is not sufficient on its own: the larger informal sector and greater inequality in the low-income country are likely to make GDP per capita both understate the typical household's consumption and overstate how widely gains are shared. The most reliable judgement comes from combining GDP per capita at PPP with HDI and a measure of inequality, and the weaker the statistical system in the low-income country, the more weight should be placed on these other indicators.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of living standards, real GDP per capita and PPP. Application: a worked PPP illustration and specific features of low-income economies (subsistence farming, mineral revenues, informal work) rather than generic points. Analysis: each point has a developed chain explaining the direction of bias (whether GDP overstates or understates the gap). Evaluation: weighs the measure against HDI and well-being data, recognises their weaknesses and reaches a supported, conditional judgement (it depends on the size of the informal sector and on inequality), which is what Level 3 evaluation requires.

check.q: Nominal GDP rises from £800bn to £864bn while the GDP deflator rises from 100 to 105. What is the approximate rate of real economic growth?
options: 3.0% fall
check.explanation: Real GDP in year 2 = 864 x 100 / 105 = £822.9bn. Growth = (822.9 - 800) / 800 x 100 = 2.9%. Nominal growth is 8%, but 5% of that is price rises.

check.q: Which situation would cause GNI to be significantly lower than GDP?
options: Large share of domestic production is owned by foreign multinationals that send profits home
Many UK residents own shares in foreign companies
The country runs a large surplus on trade in goods
The government increases spending on healthcare
check.explanation: GNI = GDP + net primary income from abroad. Profits paid to foreign owners are an outflow of primary income, so GNI falls below GDP, as in Ireland.

check.q: Why are purchasing power parity exchange rates preferred to market exchange rates when comparing living standards across countries?
options: They are set by central banks and so are more stable
They adjust for differences in the cost of living, especially of non-traded goods and services
They remove the effect of inflation within each country over time
They include the value of the informal economy
check.explanation: PPP rates equalise the cost of a common basket, so they reflect what incomes can actually buy. They do not correct for inflation over time (that is the job of real values) or for the informal economy.

check.q: Real GDP grows by 1.5% in a year while the population grows by 2%. Which statement is correct?
options: Real GDP per capita has risen by about 3.5%
Real GDP per capita has fallen by about 0.5%
The economy is in recession
Nominal GDP must have fallen
check.explanation: Real GDP per capita growth is approximately real GDP growth minus population growth: 1.5% - 2% = -0.5%. Total real output is still rising, so this is not a recession.

check.q: Which of these would increase measured UK GDP but probably reduce well-being?
options: Parent stops paid work to care for their own children
Rise in voluntary work
Spending on repairing homes after widespread flooding
An improvement in the quality of free online services
check.explanation: Repair spending adds to recorded output, but it only restores what was lost, so welfare is lower than before the flood. The other options either reduce GDP or are not captured by it.

title: Inflation
overview: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money. This topic covers how inflation is measured in the UK (constructing a weighted price index, CPI vs RPI), the three causes in the specification (demand-pull, cost-push and growth of the money supply) and the effects on consumers, firms, government and workers. The UK's surge to over 11% inflation in 2022 and the Bank of England's response give you a rich, recent case study for both data-response and essay questions.
objectives: Define inflation, deflation and disinflation precisely and interpret price index data.
Explain how the CPI is constructed (survey, basket, weights, price collection) and calculate a weighted price index.
Compare CPI and RPI and explain the limitations of price indices.
Analyse demand-pull, cost-push and monetary causes of inflation using AD/AS diagrams.
Evaluate the effects of inflation and deflation on different economic agents and on the macroeconomy.

sections.heading: Inflation, deflation and disinflation
sections.body:
**Inflation** is a sustained increase in the general (average) price level over time. It is measured as the percentage change in a price index over a year: if the CPI rises from 125.0 to 130.0, inflation is (130 - 125) / 125 x 100 = 4.0%. The key consequence is a fall in the **purchasing power of money**: each pound buys fewer goods and services.

Three related terms are frequently confused:
- **Deflation** is a sustained fall in the general price level (negative inflation). The UK had a brief period of slightly negative CPI inflation in 2015, largely because of falling oil and food prices.
- **Disinflation** is a fall in the rate of inflation while it stays positive. When UK CPI inflation fell from 11.1% in October 2022 to around 4% by late 2023, prices were still rising, just more slowly. Prices did not fall.
- **Hyperinflation** is extremely rapid inflation (often defined as over 50% a month), as in Zimbabwe in 2008 or Venezuela in the late 2010s, where money loses its functions as a store of value and unit of account.

The UK government sets the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee a **symmetric target of 2% CPI inflation**. Symmetric means undershooting is treated as seriously as overshooting. If inflation is more than 1 percentage point away from target, the Governor must write an open letter to the Chancellor explaining why and what the MPC will do. The target is 2% rather than zero because indices tend to overstate true inflation slightly, because some inflation lets real wages adjust without nominal pay cuts, and because a positive interest rate gives room to cut rates in a downturn.

sections.heading: How the CPI is constructed
sections.body:
The Consumer Prices Index measures the change in the price of a representative basket of goods and services bought by households. Constructing it involves four steps:
- **Household spending survey.** Information on what households buy comes from the Living Costs and Food Survey and national accounts data on household spending. This determines what goes in the basket and the **weights**: the share of total spending on each item.
- **The basket.** Around 700 representative items are chosen. The basket is reviewed each year to reflect changing spending: for example, air fryers were added in 2024 as households sought cheaper ways to cook, while items that have fallen out of use are removed.
- **Price collection.** Prices are collected each month from shops across the UK and online, roughly 180,000 price quotes in total, increasingly supplemented by scanner and web data.
- **Weighting and calculation.** Price changes for each item are multiplied by the item's weight, so a 10% rise in the price of something households spend a lot on (such as energy) affects the index far more than a 10% rise in the price of something minor (such as matches).

**Worked example (weighted index).** A simplified basket has three categories:
- Food: weight 20, price index rises from 100 to 110 (+10%).
- Transport: weight 30, price index falls from 100 to 95 (-5%).
- Housing and energy: weight 50, price index rises from 100 to 104 (+4%).

Weighted index = (20 x 110 + 30 x 95 + 50 x 104) / 100 = (2,200 + 2,850 + 5,200) / 100 = 102.5. Inflation = 2.5%. Notice that an unweighted average of the three changes would be (10 - 5 + 4) / 3 = 3.0%, which overstates inflation because food has a small weight. Weights must always sum to the total (here 100) before you divide.

The same method answers a common Section A question: if one item's price rises by x% and its weight is w out of 1,000, its contribution to inflation is x multiplied by w / 1,000.

sections.heading: CPI, CPIH and RPI, and the limits of price indices
sections.body:
The UK publishes several measures:
- **CPI** uses an internationally harmonised method, so it can be compared with other countries' inflation rates. It is the Bank of England's target measure. It excludes most owner-occupier housing costs such as mortgage interest payments and council tax.
- **CPIH** is CPI plus owner-occupiers' housing costs (estimated using the rent people would pay for an equivalent home) and council tax. The ONS treats CPIH as its lead measure.
- **RPI** is the older index. It includes mortgage interest payments and council tax, and uses a different averaging formula (arithmetic means at the lowest level), which makes RPI typically higher than CPI. This so-called formula effect is one reason RPI lost its status as a national statistic in 2013. RPI is still used for some contracts, index-linked gilts, student loan interest and regulated rail fares, and is due to be aligned with CPIH from 2030.

Because RPI includes mortgage interest, raising Bank Rate pushes RPI up directly, which is perverse for a measure used to judge whether monetary policy is working. That is a strong reason to target CPI.

**Limitations of any price index:**
- **Not representative of every household.** A pensioner spending heavily on energy and food, or a low-income household, faces a different inflation rate from the average. In 2022 low-income households experienced higher effective inflation because energy and food form a bigger share of their budgets.
- **Quality changes.** If a laptop's price is unchanged but it is twice as powerful, its quality-adjusted price has fallen. Statisticians attempt hedonic adjustment, but quality is hard to measure, so indices may overstate inflation.
- **Substitution bias.** Households switch towards goods whose relative price has fallen, but weights only update annually.
- **New products and shrinkflation.** New goods enter the basket with a lag; smaller pack sizes at the same price are a hidden price rise that must be tracked carefully.

sections.heading: Demand-pull inflation
sections.body:
**Demand-pull inflation** occurs when aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's ability to supply output. It is often summarised as 'too much money chasing too few goods'.

On an AD/AS diagram (see diagrams), an increase in AD from AD1 to AD2 moves the economy along an upward-sloping SRAS curve. Real output rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level rises from P1 to P2. The closer the economy is to full capacity, the steeper SRAS becomes and the more of any increase in AD shows up as inflation rather than output. This is why demand-pull inflation is associated with a **positive output gap**.

Causes of rising AD include:
- Lower interest rates or quantitative easing, which boost borrowing, asset prices and spending.
- Rising consumer confidence or wealth (for example a house price boom).
- Expansionary fiscal policy: tax cuts or higher government spending.
- Rapid growth in export demand or a depreciation of the exchange rate.

Demand-pull inflation tends to be self-reinforcing through **expectations**. If firms and workers expect higher inflation, workers bargain for higher money wages and firms raise prices in anticipation, which can create a **wage-price spiral** that pushes up both AD and costs. This is why central banks place so much weight on keeping inflation expectations anchored at the target.

sections.heading: Cost-push inflation
sections.body:
**Cost-push inflation** occurs when firms' costs of production rise and they pass these costs on as higher prices. On an AD/AS diagram, SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2: the price level rises from P1 to P2 and real output falls from Y1 to Y2. This combination of rising prices and falling output is often called **stagflation**, and it creates a painful dilemma for policy makers because measures to reduce inflation also deepen the fall in output.

Sources of cost-push pressure:
- **Commodity and energy prices.** Oil and gas are inputs to almost every industry. After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, European wholesale gas prices rose several-fold, driving up household energy bills, transport and food production costs.
- **Wage costs.** Rises in money wages not matched by productivity raise unit labour costs. Big increases in the National Living Wage, or a tight labour market, can contribute.
- **Import prices and the exchange rate.** A depreciation of sterling raises the price of imported raw materials, components and finished goods. After the 2016 referendum sterling fell sharply and UK CPI rose to around 3% by late 2017.
- **Indirect taxes and regulation.** A VAT rise or new excise duty increases prices directly; for instance the VAT rise from 17.5% to 20% in 2011 pushed inflation up temporarily.
- **Supply chain disruption.** Shipping costs and shortages of components (such as semiconductors) in 2021 raised costs worldwide.

Cost-push shocks are often **one-off changes in the price level**: once energy prices stop rising, measured inflation falls back (base effects). Inflation only persists if the shock feeds into wages and expectations (second-round effects).

sections.heading: Growth of the money supply
sections.body:
The third cause in the specification is excessive growth of the money supply, the monetarist explanation. The **quantity theory of money** starts from the identity MV = PY, where M is the money supply, V the velocity of circulation (how many times each pound is spent in a year), P the price level and Y real output. Monetarists such as Milton Friedman argued that V is fairly stable and Y is determined by supply-side factors in the long run, so a faster growth of M must lead to a faster rise in P. In their words, inflation is 'always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon'.

**Worked example.** If M grows by 10%, V is constant and real output grows by 2%, then P must rise by roughly 10% - 2% = 8%.

Critics, mainly Keynesians, argue that V is not stable (it fell sharply after 2008 as banks and households hoarded money), and that if there is spare capacity extra money can raise Y rather than P. The experience after 2009 supports them: the Bank of England created hundreds of billions of pounds of reserves through QE, yet inflation stayed low through the 2010s.

However, monetarists point to 2020 to 2022: broad money grew at double-digit rates in 2020 as QE (which eventually totalled £895bn) coincided with large government borrowing, and inflation surged roughly two years later. A balanced answer is that money supply growth is most inflationary when the economy is near full capacity and when it finances spending directly, and that it is difficult to separate its effect from simultaneous demand and cost shocks.

sections.heading: Effects of inflation and deflation
sections.body:
The effects depend on whether inflation is **anticipated** (correctly expected and built into contracts) or **unanticipated**, and on how high and volatile it is.

**Consumers and households**
- Falling real incomes for anyone whose income rises more slowly than prices: workers without strong bargaining power, savers, and those on fixed incomes.
- **Savers** lose if the interest rate is below inflation (negative real interest rate). **Borrowers** gain because the real value of debt falls.
- Arbitrary **redistribution** from creditors to debtors and from those on fixed incomes to those with index-linked incomes.

**Firms**
- **Menu costs** of changing prices and **shoe-leather costs** of managing cash more actively.
- Uncertainty makes it harder to plan, so investment may fall, damaging long-run growth.
- Loss of **international price competitiveness** if UK inflation exceeds that of trading partners (unless offset by depreciation), worsening the current account.

**Government**
- **Fiscal drag**: if tax thresholds are frozen, inflation pulls more people into higher tax bands, raising revenue. UK income tax thresholds were frozen from 2021, so high inflation sharply increased the real tax take.
- Higher spending on index-linked benefits and pensions, and higher interest costs on index-linked gilts.
- The real value of government debt is reduced.

**Workers** may gain in nominal terms if unions negotiate pay rises, but frequently suffer **real wage cuts**, as in 2022 to 2023 when UK real pay fell.

**Deflation** can be good if caused by falling costs or rising productivity (benign deflation). But demand-led deflation is dangerous: consumers postpone purchases expecting lower prices, the real value of debt rises, firms cut output and wages, and nominal interest rates cannot fall below about zero, so monetary policy becomes less effective. Japan's experience of weak growth and falling prices from the 1990s is the standard example.

key_terms.definition: A sustained increase in the general price level over time, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
A sustained fall in the general price level over time (negative inflation).
A fall in the rate of inflation, so prices are still rising but more slowly.
A weighted index of the prices of a representative basket of consumer goods and services; the measure targeted by the Bank of England at 2%.
An older UK price index that includes mortgage interest payments and council tax and uses a different formula, so it is typically higher than CPI.
The proportion of total household spending on each item or category in the basket, used so that changes in more important items have a bigger effect on the index.
Inflation caused by aggregate demand growing faster than the economy's capacity to supply output.
Inflation caused by rising costs of production, such as wages, energy or imported raw materials, which shift SRAS to the left.
The theory based on MV = PY that, with velocity and real output stable, growth of the money supply causes proportionate inflation.
A process in which higher prices lead workers to demand higher wages, which raise firms' costs and so prices further.
The rise in the real tax burden when tax thresholds are not raised in line with inflation, so more income is taxed at higher rates.
The nominal interest rate minus the rate of inflation; it shows the true return to savers and cost to borrowers.
A combination of high inflation and stagnant or falling output with rising unemployment, typically caused by a cost-push shock.

diagrams.title: Demand-pull inflation
diagrams.caption: An increase in aggregate demand from AD1 to AD2 moves the economy up SRAS: the price level rises from P1 to P2 and real output rises from Y1 to Y2. Nearer full capacity, SRAS is steeper and more of the rise in AD becomes inflation.

diagrams.title: Cost-push inflation
diagrams.caption: Higher costs of production (for example energy prices) shift SRAS left from SRAS1 to SRAS2. The price level rises from P1 to P2 while real output falls from Y1 to Y2: stagflation.

formulae.name: Rate of inflation
formulae.formula: (Price index this year - price index last year) / price index last year x 100
formulae.example: CPI rises from 125.0 to 130.0: inflation = 5 / 125 x 100 = 4.0%.

formulae.name: Weighted price index
formulae.formula: Sum of (weight x item price index) / sum of weights

formulae.name: Contribution of one item
formulae.formula: Percentage price change x (item weight / total weight)
formulae.example: Energy weight 60 out of 1,000 rises 50% in price: contribution = 50 x 0.06 = 3 percentage points of inflation.

formulae.name: Real interest rate
formulae.formula: Nominal interest rate - inflation rate
formulae.example: Savings rate 4%, inflation 6%: real interest rate = -2%, so savings lose purchasing power.

formulae.name: Quantity theory of money
formulae.formula: MV = PY, so %ΔP ≈ %ΔM + %ΔV - %ΔY
formulae.example: Money supply +10%, velocity constant, real output +2%: inflation ≈ 8%.

applications: UK CPI inflation rose from under 1% in early 2021 to a peak of 11.1% in October 2022, the highest for about 40 years. The biggest contributors were household energy and then food, whose annual inflation came close to 20% in early 2023. The government's Energy Price Guarantee, which limited a typical household's annual bill to around £2,500 from October 2022, stopped measured inflation peaking even higher.

The Bank of England raised Bank Rate fourteen times in a row, from 0.1% in December 2021 to 5.25% in August 2023, to stop the energy shock becoming persistent through wages and expectations. Inflation fell back to the 2% target briefly in mid-2024 as energy prices fell (base effects), then rose back to almost 4% in 2025, partly because of regulated prices and food costs, illustrating how hard the last stretch of disinflation can be.

Index-linking in the UK: most working-age benefits are uprated each April by the previous September's CPI, the state pension is uprated under the triple lock (the highest of earnings growth, CPI inflation or 2.5%), and index-linked gilts pay returns linked to RPI. High inflation therefore raises government spending as well as tax revenue through fiscal drag.

Globally, the post-pandemic surge was shared across advanced economies (US CPI inflation peaked around 9% in mid-2022 and euro area inflation exceeded 10%), suggesting common cost-push shocks. But the US experienced more demand-pull pressure after very large fiscal stimulus, which is why US core inflation rose earlier.

Japan provides the contrasting case of persistent low inflation and periods of deflation from the late 1990s, during which consumers delayed spending and the Bank of Japan kept interest rates around zero for decades.
evaluation: Causes are rarely separable: in 2021 to 2023 cost-push (energy, supply chains) and demand-pull (post-lockdown spending, savings built up during lockdowns, QE) operated together, and second-round effects through wages blurred the line further. A strong answer weighs which dominated at which stage.

Magnitude and persistence matter more than the existence of inflation: steady, predictable inflation of 2% imposes small costs, whereas high and volatile inflation causes uncertainty, arbitrary redistribution and lower investment.
Anticipated vs unanticipated: if inflation is fully anticipated and contracts are index-linked, redistribution effects are small; the costs are largest when inflation is a surprise.

Stakeholders differ: borrowers with fixed-rate mortgages and the government (via fiscal drag and erosion of debt) can gain, while savers, people on fixed incomes and low-income households with high energy and food shares lose most.

Deflation is not always harmful: falling prices driven by productivity improvements (benign deflation) can raise real incomes, while demand-driven deflation is damaging. Always identify the cause before judging the effect.
The monetarist link from money to prices holds better in the long run and near full capacity than in a slump with high spare capacity, where velocity tends to fall.
misconceptions: Saying prices fall when inflation falls. A fall in inflation from 10% to 4% is disinflation; prices are still rising by 4% a year.
Calculating a simple average of price changes instead of using the weights. Always multiply each change by its weight and divide by the sum of weights.
Drawing cost-push inflation as a shift of AD, or showing output rising. Cost-push shifts SRAS left, so output falls as the price level rises.
Assuming inflation always makes everyone worse off. Debtors and those with index-linked or rising incomes can gain; the effects are redistributive.
Describing RPI as the inflation target. The Bank of England targets CPI at 2%; RPI includes mortgage interest so it moves when Bank Rate changes.
exam_tips: Section A questions often give an index table and weights. Show the formula, compute each step and state the answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
Always draw and label the AD/AS diagram accurately: axes as price level and real output (not price and quantity), equilibrium points, and the direction of the shift with an arrow.

For 25-mark essays on causes, give the mechanism for each cause, apply it to a specific UK period (2011 VAT rise, 2017 depreciation, 2022 energy shock), then evaluate by judging relative importance and persistence.

When discussing effects, organise by stakeholder (consumers, savers, borrowers, firms, government, workers) and finish with a judgement that depends on the rate, volatility and whether it was anticipated.
Synoptic links: monetary policy and the MPC (2.6.2), Phillips curve trade-offs (2.6.4), international competitiveness and exchange rates (4.1.8, 4.1.9), and the role of central banks (4.4.3).

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that the rise in UK inflation between 2021 and 2023 was mainly caused by cost-push factors. (25 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured in the UK by the Consumer Prices Index. CPI inflation rose from below 1% in early 2021 to a peak of 11.1% in October 2022, before falling back during 2023. Cost-push inflation is caused by rising costs of production shifting short-run aggregate supply to the left, whereas demand-pull inflation is caused by aggregate demand rising faster than productive capacity. A third explanation is excessive growth in the money supply.

The strongest case for cost-push is energy. After Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, European wholesale gas prices rose several-fold. Energy is an input into nearly all production: manufacturing, transport, food processing and heating commercial premises. As firms' costs rose, SRAS shifted left from SRAS1 to SRAS2: the price level rose from P1 to P2 and real output fell from Y1 to Y2. This is consistent with what happened in the UK, where output stagnated during late 2022 and 2023 while inflation was at its highest. The effect was magnified because household energy has a significant weight in the CPI basket, so a doubling of household energy prices directly contributed several percentage points to measured inflation, even after the Energy Price Guarantee limited the typical annual bill to around £2,500. Food prices followed, with food inflation close to 20% in early 2023, reflecting energy-intensive fertiliser production and the disruption of Ukrainian grain exports.

A second cost-push factor was global supply chain disruption in 2021. As economies reopened after lockdowns, shortages of shipping containers and semiconductors raised costs and delayed deliveries. In addition, a weaker pound against the dollar in 2022, briefly falling to a record low after the September mini-budget, raised the sterling price of dollar-denominated commodities such as oil, adding to imported cost pressure. Finally, a tight labour market, with high vacancies and rising economic inactivity, pushed up money wages. If wages rise faster than productivity, unit labour costs increase, which can cause a wage-price spiral as workers try to restore their real pay.

However, there is a strong case that demand-side factors were also important. During lockdowns households accumulated large excess savings because spending opportunities were restricted, while incomes were protected by the furlough scheme. When restrictions ended in 2021, pent-up spending boosted consumption, a component of AD. At the same time Bank Rate was at a record low of 0.1% and the Bank of England had expanded quantitative easing to a total of £895bn, so credit was cheap and asset prices were high, supporting wealth effects. On an AD/AS diagram, AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2 along an upward-sloping SRAS; because the economy was recovering quickly towards capacity and supply was constrained, SRAS was steep, so much of the rise in AD showed up as higher prices. Monetarists would add that broad money grew at double-digit rates in 2020, and, using MV = PY, with real output constrained, faster monetary growth would eventually raise the price level. The fact that UK inflation was already above 5% by the end of 2021, before the invasion, suggests demand was playing a role before the largest energy shock.

Evaluating the relative importance, the timing is crucial. In 2021 the rise was a mix of demand recovery and supply-chain cost pressures. In 2022 the energy shock dominated: the largest single contributions to the October 2022 peak came from household energy and food, which are classic cost-push items, and the shock was common to countries with very different fiscal and monetary policies, which points to a global supply cause rather than domestic excess demand. The output evidence also supports cost-push: if inflation had been mainly demand-pull, real output would have been rising strongly, whereas the UK economy was broadly stagnant in 2022 to 2023.

However, the persistence of inflation in 2023 tells a different story. As energy prices fell, headline inflation dropped, but services inflation, which mostly reflects domestic wage costs, stayed high at around 6 to 7%. This suggests second-round effects from the tight labour market and inflation expectations. These were initially triggered by cost-push shocks but sustained by domestic demand and wage bargaining. This also explains the Bank of England's decision to raise Bank Rate fourteen times to 5.25%: monetary policy cannot stop an energy price shock, but it can prevent the shock from becoming embedded in wage settlements and expectations.

In conclusion, the view is largely correct for the peak of inflation in 2022, when energy and food costs, external supply shocks and a weaker pound shifted SRAS left and drove the price level up while output stagnated. But cost-push is not the whole story. Loose monetary policy, the release of pandemic savings and a tight labour market meant demand was strong enough for firms to pass on higher costs and for wages to follow, which made inflation more persistent. The most accurate judgement is that cost-push factors were the main trigger, while demand-side and monetary conditions determined how high and how long-lasting inflation became.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge and application: accurate definitions of all three causes, with precise UK evidence (11.1% peak, 0.1% to 5.25% Bank Rate, £895bn QE, energy guarantee, services inflation). Analysis: two AD/AS diagrams are referenced with full chains of reasoning, plus the quantity theory and the wage-price spiral mechanism. Evaluation: judges relative importance by timing (2021 vs 2022 vs 2023), uses output and international evidence to discriminate between causes, distinguishes trigger from persistence and reaches a nuanced, supported conclusion, meeting Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

check.q: A price index rises from 240 to 252. What is the rate of inflation?
check.explanation: (252 - 240) / 240 x 100 = 12 / 240 x 100 = 5%. A 12-point rise is not a 12% rise unless the index was at 100.

check.q: In a CPI basket, energy has a weight of 50 out of 1,000. If energy prices rise by 40% and all other prices are unchanged, by how much does CPI rise?
check.explanation: Contribution = 40% x 50 / 1,000 = 2 percentage points. Weights determine how much each price change matters for the overall index.

check.q: UK CPI inflation falls from 6.7% to 3.9%. What has happened to the price level?
options: It has fallen
It has continued to rise, but more slowly
It has stayed constant
It has risen faster than before
check.explanation: This is disinflation. Inflation remains positive, so prices are still rising, just at a slower rate.

check.q: Which of the following is most likely to cause cost-push inflation in the UK?
options: Cut in Bank Rate
Rise in consumer confidence
Depreciation of sterling
An increase in house prices
check.explanation: A depreciation raises the sterling price of imported raw materials, energy and components, shifting SRAS left. The other three raise AD and so cause demand-pull pressure.

check.q: Why does the Bank of England target CPI rather than RPI?
options: RPI excludes food and energy prices
RPI includes mortgage interest payments, so raising Bank Rate would directly increase measured inflation
CPI includes owner-occupier housing costs, which RPI excludes
RPI is calculated only once a year
check.explanation: Because RPI includes mortgage interest payments, tightening monetary policy pushes RPI up in the short term, which would make it a misleading target. CPI also follows international methods, allowing comparisons.

title: Employment and unemployment
overview: Unemployment is one of the most visible measures of how well an economy is performing, and it has serious costs for individuals, firms, government and society. This topic covers how unemployment is measured in the UK (claimant count vs the ILO Labour Force Survey measure), the difference between unemployment, underemployment and economic inactivity, the causes and types of unemployment, and the significance of migration for the labour market. Examiners regularly test calculations of rates, the distinction between types, and evaluation of the effects of migration and of rising unemployment.
objectives: Distinguish employment, unemployment, underemployment and economic inactivity, and calculate the relevant rates.
Compare the claimant count and the ILO measure and explain the strengths and weaknesses of each.
Explain and illustrate the causes of unemployment: frictional, structural, seasonal, cyclical and real-wage (classical) unemployment.
Analyse the significance of changes in employment, unemployment and inactivity rates.
Evaluate the effects of unemployment and of migration on the UK economy.

sections.heading: Key definitions and how to calculate rates
sections.body:
The population of working age is divided into three groups:
- **Employed**: people doing paid work, including part-time and self-employed work (one hour a week counts).
- **Unemployed**: people without a job who want one, are available to start and are actively seeking work.
- **Economically inactive**: people neither working nor seeking work, such as full-time students, those looking after family, the long-term sick and early retirees.

The **labour force** (economically active population) is the employed plus the unemployed. The rates are calculated on different bases:
- Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force x 100.
- Employment rate = employed / population aged 16 to 64 x 100.
- Inactivity rate = inactive / population aged 16 to 64 x 100.

**Worked example.** Population aged 16 to 64 = 42.0m. Employed = 31.5m. Unemployed = 1.5m.
- Labour force = 33.0m; inactive = 42.0 - 33.0 = 9.0m.
- Unemployment rate = 1.5 / 33.0 x 100 = 4.5%.
- Employment rate = 31.5 / 42.0 x 100 = 75.0%.
- Inactivity rate = 9.0 / 42.0 x 100 = 21.4%.

These numbers are close to recent UK values. The crucial insight: the unemployment rate can fall even if employment falls, if people leave the labour force altogether (for example because of long-term sickness). After the pandemic UK inactivity rose, with the number inactive because of long-term sickness reaching around 2.8 million in 2024. A low unemployment rate in that situation is not a sign of a healthy labour market.

**Underemployment** describes people who are employed but would like to work more hours, or who are working in jobs below their skill level (for example a graduate in a role that requires no qualifications). The ILO unemployment rate does not capture this, so it can understate spare capacity in the labour market, particularly when part-time and zero-hours contracts are common.

sections.heading: Measuring unemployment: claimant count vs ILO
sections.body:
**The claimant count** measures the number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits: Jobseeker's Allowance plus those on Universal Credit who are required to look for work. It is a by-product of the benefits system, so it is cheap, available monthly and available for small local areas.

Weaknesses:
- It excludes people who are unemployed but not entitled to or not claiming benefits, such as people with a working partner, those with savings above the limit, many 16 to 17 year olds and people who choose not to claim.
- It changes whenever benefit rules change, so it is unreliable over time. Under Universal Credit, some people in low-paid work are also required to search for more work and appear in the count, which inflated it after 2020.
- Governments can be accused of manipulating it by changing eligibility rules, as happened many times in the 1980s and 1990s.

**The ILO measure** comes from the Labour Force Survey (LFS), a large quarterly household survey. A person is ILO unemployed if they are without a job, have actively sought work in the past four weeks and are available to start within two weeks (or are waiting to start a job already obtained). The headline UK unemployment rate is the ILO rate.

Strengths: it follows an international definition, so it can be compared across countries and is not affected by benefit rule changes. Weaknesses: it is a sample survey, so it has sampling error and is more expensive to collect; small month-to-month changes are often not statistically significant. In 2023 the LFS response rate fell so far that the ONS temporarily suspended some estimates and flagged the data as less reliable, while it develops a transformed survey. Policy makers such as the MPC have therefore had to triangulate with payroll (HMRC PAYE) data, vacancies and business surveys.

Usually the ILO count is higher than the claimant count because it includes people not entitled to benefits, but the gap has narrowed under Universal Credit.

sections.heading: Frictional, seasonal and structural unemployment
sections.body:
**Frictional unemployment** is short-term unemployment while people move between jobs or enter the labour market (for example graduates searching for their first role). It exists because information is imperfect: it takes time to match workers to vacancies. Some frictional unemployment is healthy, as it improves the quality of job matches. It can be reduced by better information (online job platforms, Jobcentre Plus) and by reducing the **unemployment trap**, where benefits withdrawn on taking a job reduce the incentive to search quickly.

**Seasonal unemployment** occurs because demand for some labour varies predictably with the season: tourism in coastal towns, agriculture, construction in winter, and retail after Christmas. Official statistics are seasonally adjusted to show the underlying trend.

**Structural unemployment** is long-term unemployment caused by a mismatch between the skills or location of workers and the jobs available. It arises from changes in the structure of the economy, such as the decline of an industry because of technological change or foreign competition. It persists because of:
- **Occupational immobility**: workers lack the skills for available jobs (a former steelworker cannot easily become a software engineer).
- **Geographical immobility**: high housing costs in London and the South East, family ties and differences between regions make it hard to move to where jobs are.

UK examples include the decline of coal mining and manufacturing in the 1980s, the closure of blast furnaces at Port Talbot in 2024 with the loss of roughly 2,800 jobs announced by Tata Steel, and the potential for automation and artificial intelligence to replace routine administrative tasks. Structural unemployment is often concentrated regionally, which explains persistent differences in unemployment and inactivity between regions. Policies to tackle it are supply-side: training, apprenticeships, regional investment and housing reform.

sections.heading: Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment
sections.body:
**Cyclical unemployment**, also called demand-deficient or Keynesian unemployment, occurs when aggregate demand falls, as in a recession. Firms sell less, so the demand for labour (a **derived demand**) falls and firms cut hours, stop hiring and make workers redundant.

On an AD/AS diagram, a fall in AD from AD1 to AD2 reduces real output from the full-employment level Yfe to Y2, creating a **negative output gap**. The gap between Y2 and Yfe represents output that is not produced because labour and capital are idle. Unemployment rose sharply in the UK after the 2008 financial crisis, peaking at around 8% in 2011, and in the early 1980s and early 1990s recessions it rose above 10%.

Cyclical unemployment can be tackled by demand-side policies: lower interest rates, quantitative easing, higher government spending or tax cuts. During the pandemic the furlough scheme (Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme), which paid up to 80% of wages for millions of workers, prevented a large rise in cyclical unemployment by keeping workers attached to their employers: ILO unemployment peaked at only around 5% despite an unprecedented fall in output.

A crucial evaluation point is **hysteresis**: if cyclical unemployment lasts long enough, the long-term unemployed lose skills, motivation and work habits, and employers become reluctant to hire them. Cyclical unemployment then becomes structural, reducing the economy's productive capacity (LRAS shifts left). This is a strong argument for rapid demand-side responses to recessions.

sections.heading: Real-wage inflexibility (classical unemployment)
sections.body:
Classical economists argue that unemployment arises when the **real wage is held above the market-clearing level**. In the labour market diagram, the demand for labour slopes down (firms hire more workers at lower real wages) and the supply of labour slopes up. At the equilibrium real wage W* everyone who wants to work at that wage is employed (apart from frictional unemployment).

If the real wage is fixed at W1 above W*, firms demand only QD workers while QS want to work. The excess supply of labour (QS - QD) is real-wage unemployment. The real wage might be kept above equilibrium by:
- A **national minimum wage** set too high relative to productivity.
- **Trade union** bargaining power.
- **Downward wage stickiness**: firms are reluctant to cut nominal pay because it damages morale, and contracts fix wages for a period.

Evaluation: evidence on the UK National Minimum Wage, introduced in 1999, and the National Living Wage since 2016, suggests the employment effects have been small so far, partly because firms have responded by raising prices, accepting lower profits, improving productivity, or because employers have some monopsony power (in which case a minimum wage can raise employment). The Low Pay Commission monitors this carefully, especially for young workers and small firms in low-margin sectors such as hospitality. Note also that inflation erodes real wages when nominal wages are sticky, which is one argument for a positive inflation target.

sections.heading: The significance of migration
sections.body:
Migration affects both the supply of labour and the demand for labour, so its effect on unemployment is not straightforward.

**Effects that could raise unemployment for existing workers:**
- Inward migration increases the supply of labour. In the short run, if wages are sticky and demand does not keep up, competition for jobs may rise, especially in low-skilled sectors.
- Some studies suggest small downward pressure on wages for the lowest-paid workers in sectors with high inflows.

**Effects that reduce or offset unemployment:**
- Migrants also spend their incomes, raising consumption and AD, which increases the demand for labour. The lump of labour fallacy is the mistaken belief that there is a fixed number of jobs.
- Migrants often fill skill shortages (for example in the NHS and social care, where the health and care visa has been heavily used), which allows firms to expand and can create complementary jobs for UK workers.
- Migrants tend to be of working age and have high employment rates, raising tax revenue and potential output (LRAS shifts right).

**UK evidence.** Net migration rose to an unprecedented level of roughly 900,000 in the year to mid-2023 under the post-Brexit points-based system, driven by work visas, students and humanitarian routes, before falling sharply to roughly half that level in 2024 after visa rules were tightened (including a higher skilled worker salary threshold from 2024). Most UK studies find little or no overall effect of migration on the unemployment rate of UK-born workers. However, very rapid population growth raised total GDP while GDP per capita stagnated, and placed pressure on housing and public services, which affects the political debate.

**Emigration** matters too: countries that lose skilled young workers (a brain drain) can suffer skill shortages, although remittances sent home can partly compensate.

sections.heading: Effects of unemployment
sections.body:
Unemployment imposes costs on many stakeholders:
- **Unemployed individuals**: loss of income, savings run down, worse physical and mental health, loss of skills (hysteresis) and lower future earnings (scarring, especially for young people who are unemployed early in their careers).
- **Firms**: lower consumer spending reduces sales and profits, especially for firms selling income-elastic goods. However, firms find it easier to recruit and face less wage pressure.
- **Government**: lower income tax and VAT receipts plus higher spending on benefits (automatic stabilisers) widen the budget deficit and increase borrowing. There may be higher spending on health and policing.
- **Society**: greater inequality and poverty, regional decline, and higher crime in areas of persistent unemployment.
- **The economy**: output is below potential (inside the PPF), so resources are wasted. This is a pure opportunity cost: the lost output can never be recovered.

The size of these costs depends on the **duration** (long-term unemployment of over 12 months is far more damaging), the **type** (frictional unemployment has small costs and some benefits), and the **distribution** (concentrated in particular regions or groups such as young people). Some economists also argue that a modest level of unemployment helps keep inflation under control, which links to the Phillips curve trade-off in 2.6.4.

key_terms.definition: People of working age who are without a job, available for work and actively seeking work.
A situation where people are employed but want to work more hours, or are working in jobs that do not use their skills and qualifications.
People of working age who are neither in work nor seeking work, such as students, carers and the long-term sick.
A measure of unemployment based on the number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits.
A survey-based measure of people without a job who have sought work in the past four weeks and are available to start within two weeks.
Short-term unemployment while people search for or move between jobs, caused by imperfect information.
Long-term unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the jobs available, often after the decline of an industry.
Unemployment caused by predictable seasonal changes in the demand for labour.
Unemployment caused by a lack of aggregate demand, typically in a downturn or recession.
Unemployment caused by the real wage being held above the market-clearing level, creating an excess supply of labour.
The process by which a temporary rise in unemployment becomes persistent because the unemployed lose skills and employability.
The difficulty workers face in moving between jobs that require different skills.
The difficulty workers face in moving to areas where jobs are available, for example because of housing costs or family ties.

diagrams.title: Cyclical unemployment: a fall in AD
diagrams.caption: A fall in AD from AD1 to AD2 reduces real output from the full-employment level Yfe to Y2. The negative output gap (Yfe - Y2) means fewer workers are needed, so cyclical unemployment rises.

diagrams.title: Real-wage (classical) unemployment
diagrams.caption: At the market-clearing real wage W* the labour market clears at Q*. If the real wage is held at W1 (by a minimum wage, union power or sticky wages), firms employ only QD while QS want to work: the excess supply a to b is real-wage unemployment.

formulae.name: Unemployment rate
formulae.formula: Number unemployed / labour force (employed + unemployed) x 100

formulae.name: Employment rate
formulae.formula: Number employed aged 16 to 64 / population aged 16 to 64 x 100

formulae.name: Inactivity rate
formulae.formula: Number inactive aged 16 to 64 / population aged 16 to 64 x 100

applications: UK ILO unemployment fell to around 3.6 to 4% in 2022, its lowest for about 50 years, while vacancies peaked at roughly 1.3 million. This was not simply a booming economy: rising economic inactivity, particularly long-term sickness, reduced labour supply, creating labour shortages and wage pressure. Unemployment then drifted up towards 5% during 2025 as the labour market loosened.

The furlough scheme (2020 to 2021) protected around 11 million jobs at different points by paying up to 80% of wages. ILO unemployment peaked at only around 5% despite GDP falling by around 10% in 2020, showing how policy can prevent cyclical unemployment from turning into long-term structural unemployment.

Structural change continues: the end of blast-furnace steelmaking at Port Talbot in 2024 and the shift to electric arc furnaces cost thousands of jobs in a single area, while shortages persisted in care, construction and engineering. This combination of unemployment in some places with vacancies in others is the signature of structural unemployment.

Youth unemployment is typically around three times the overall rate, and the number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs) rose to almost 1 million in 2024 to 2025, raising concerns about long-term scarring effects.

Internationally, Spain's unemployment rate exceeded 25% after the euro crisis, with youth unemployment above 50%, illustrating how a large demand shock combined with rigid labour markets and no independent exchange rate can produce persistent unemployment.
evaluation: The measure matters: claimant count and ILO unemployment can move differently, and falling unemployment combined with rising inactivity may signal a weakening, not a strengthening, labour market. Look at employment and inactivity rates as well.

Type determines policy: cyclical unemployment responds to demand-side policy, but structural unemployment requires supply-side measures that take years to work. Using demand stimulus against structural unemployment mainly causes inflation.
Duration and distribution determine the cost: short frictional spells are low cost or even beneficial, while long-term and youth unemployment have scarring effects and hysteresis.
Data reliability: the falling LFS response rate since 2023 means recent UK unemployment estimates carry wider margins of error, so conclusions drawn from small changes should be cautious.

Migration effects depend on the skills mix of migrants relative to UK workers, the state of the economy (spare capacity or full employment) and the time period: short-run competition effects tend to be offset by higher demand and output in the long run.
Minimum wage effects depend on the level relative to median earnings, the elasticity of labour demand and whether employers have monopsony power.
misconceptions: Calculating the unemployment rate as a percentage of the whole population or of the working-age population. The denominator is the labour force (employed plus unemployed).
Assuming that everyone without a job is unemployed. Students, carers and the long-term sick who are not seeking work are economically inactive.
Describing unemployment caused by technology or deindustrialisation as cyclical. If the jobs have permanently disappeared it is structural, even if it began in a recession.
Arguing that migrants simply take a fixed number of jobs (the lump of labour fallacy). Migrants also raise demand and so create jobs.
Treating a rise in employment and a fall in unemployment as the same thing. Both can rise together if the labour force grows, for example through migration.
exam_tips: Learn the ILO definition word-for-word: without a job, actively sought work in the last four weeks, available to start in the next two weeks.
In data questions, check the denominators and whether figures are levels (millions) or rates (%). A rise in the number unemployed can coincide with a stable rate if the labour force is growing.

When asked to explain a cause of unemployment, identify the type, explain the mechanism and support it with a UK example. For cyclical unemployment always link to AD and derived demand; for real-wage unemployment use the labour market diagram.
For evaluation of migration or unemployment, use stakeholders, short run vs long run and the magnitude of the change, and reach a judgement on which effect dominates for the UK today.
Synoptic links: labour market diagrams and minimum wages (3.5.3), supply-side policies (2.6.3), the Phillips curve (2.6.4) and inequality (4.2.2).

model_answer.question: Assess the likely impact of high levels of net inward migration on unemployment in the UK. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Net inward migration is the number of people coming to live in a country minus the number leaving. Unemployment is the number of people without a job who are actively seeking work and available to start. UK net migration reached roughly 900,000 in the year to mid-2023, so its effect on the labour market is a major policy question.

The main argument that migration raises unemployment is that it increases the supply of labour. Most migrants are of working age and many come on work visas, so the labour force grows. If the demand for labour does not rise at the same pace, and wages are sticky downwards, there will be an excess supply of labour at the existing wage, which means higher unemployment. This is most likely in sectors where migrants and UK workers are close substitutes, such as low-skilled hospitality, warehousing or food processing, and in the short run when firms have not yet expanded. It may also affect particular groups such as young people looking for entry-level jobs.

However, migration also increases the demand for labour. Migrants spend their incomes on housing, food and services, raising consumption, which is a component of aggregate demand. Since the demand for labour is derived from the demand for goods and services, higher AD encourages firms to hire. The idea that there is a fixed number of jobs (the lump of labour fallacy) is therefore wrong. In addition, many migrants fill skill shortages: the NHS and social care sectors have relied heavily on health and care visas.
