diagrams.title: Investment and the interest rate
diagrams.caption: A fall in the interest rate from r1 to r2 makes more projects profitable: a movement along I1 from a to b. Greater confidence, faster expected growth or tax incentives raise expected returns at every interest rate, shifting the curve to I2 (from a to c at r1).

diagrams.title: Investment raises AD and LRAS
diagrams.caption: Higher investment shifts AD right (AD1 to AD2) as a component of spending. Over time the extra capital raises productive capacity, shifting LRAS right (LRAS1 to LRAS2), so real output can rise from Y1 to Y2 without a rise in the price level.

formulae.name: Net investment
formulae.formula: Gross investment - depreciation

formulae.name: Accelerator
formulae.formula: Net investment = capital-output ratio x change in output
formulae.example: Capital-output ratio 3, output rises £5m: net investment = 3 x 5 = £15m.

applications: UK business investment has been around 10% of GDP for many years, among the lowest in the G7. It was broadly flat between 2016 and 2019 as uncertainty about future trade with the EU led firms to delay projects, contributing to the UK's weak productivity growth.

Full expensing, made permanent in the 2023 Autumn Statement, allows companies to deduct 100% of qualifying plant and machinery investment from taxable profits immediately. It was designed to offset the rise in corporation tax to 25% and close the investment gap with other advanced economies.

The rise in Bank Rate to 5.25% in 2023 raised borrowing costs and hurdle rates, particularly for commercial property and housebuilding, where investment is most interest-sensitive. Housebuilding slowed sharply in 2023 to 2024.

In the USA, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 offered large tax credits for clean energy and electric vehicle investment, attracting investment in batteries and solar manufacturing and prompting concern in the UK and EU that investment would be diverted to the US.

Government capital spending on major projects such as HS2 shows the risks of public investment: large cost overruns and the cancellation of the northern leg in 2023 raised questions about planning and value for money.
evaluation: Interest rates matter less than theory suggests: hurdle rates are sticky and confidence often dominates, so cutting Bank Rate in a deep downturn may have little effect on investment.
The accelerator makes investment volatile, but spare capacity, expectations and financing constraints mean the relationship between output growth and investment is loose in practice.
Uncertainty has an option value: firms delay irreversible projects when the future is unclear, so policy stability can be as important as tax incentives.

Short run vs long run: investment raises AD immediately but raises LRAS only after projects are completed and operating, which can take years; the long-run supply-side benefit is the more important for living standards.
Quality matters as well as quantity: investment in obsolete technology or poorly planned infrastructure may add little to productivity.
Public investment may crowd in or crowd out private investment, depending on whether the economy has spare capacity and whether it is financed in a way that raises interest rates.
misconceptions: Calling the purchase of shares or saving in a bank investment. In economics, investment is spending on new capital goods; buying existing shares is a financial transaction.
Thinking that investment only falls when output falls. Under the accelerator, net investment falls when output growth slows.
Confusing gross and net investment. Gross includes replacement of depreciated capital; only net investment increases the capital stock.
Showing only an AD shift for investment in a long-run question. Investment also shifts LRAS, which is the more important effect for long-run growth.
Assuming lower interest rates automatically raise investment. Firms will not invest if expected demand is weak or uncertainty is high.
exam_tips: Accelerator calculations appear in Section A: set out required capital, net investment and gross investment year by year, and comment on what happens when growth slows.
Always link investment to both AD (short run, multiplier) and LRAS (long run, productivity) in essays. Drawing both shifts on one diagram is an efficient way to show this.
Use UK specifics: business investment around 10% of GDP, full expensing, corporation tax at 25%, Brexit uncertainty, planning reform. Examiners reward this precise application.
Evaluation should prioritise: which influence is most important at the time described in the extract? In a recession, confidence usually dominates interest rates.
Synoptic links: productivity and LRAS (2.3.3), the multiplier (2.4.4), the trade cycle (2.5.3), supply-side policy (2.6.3) and financial markets (4.4.1).

model_answer.question: Assess the factors that may explain the relatively low level of business investment in the UK. (15 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Business investment is spending by private firms on capital goods such as machinery, buildings, equipment and software. UK business investment has been around 10% of GDP for many years, among the lowest in the G7, which matters because investment raises both aggregate demand and, in the long run, productive capacity.

One important factor is uncertainty. Investment projects are long-term and often irreversible, so firms base decisions on expected returns over many years. When uncertainty rises, the value of waiting increases, and firms postpone projects. After the 2016 EU referendum, UK business investment was broadly flat for several years, as firms did not know what trading arrangements with the UK's largest export market would be. Subsequent policy changes, including frequent changes to tax rules and the market turmoil after the September 2022 mini-budget, may have reinforced a perception of instability. Lower expected returns or higher perceived risk reduce investment at every interest rate, shifting the investment demand curve to the left.

A second factor is the structure of the UK economy. Around 80% of UK output comes from services, many of which, such as finance, law and consulting, are less capital-intensive than manufacturing. The capital-output ratio is lower, so the same growth in output requires less physical investment. This suggests that some of the gap with countries such as Germany reflects comparative advantage rather than a weakness. However, measured investment may also understate intangible investment such as software, data and brand-building, which services firms rely on.

A third factor is weak demand growth. Under the accelerator theory, net investment depends on the rate of growth of output. UK growth since 2008 has been slow, with productivity growth of only around 0.5% a year compared with around 2% before the financial crisis. If firms expect slow growth in sales, they need little extra capacity, so net investment stays low. This creates a vicious circle: low investment causes low productivity growth, which causes slow growth, which discourages investment.

Financial and policy factors also contribute. Some economists argue that UK financial markets encourage short-termism, with shareholders prioritising dividends over long-term projects, and that smaller firms struggle to access finance. The rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25% in 2023 reduced post-tax returns, though full expensing offsets this for plant and machinery. Slow planning decisions and difficulty obtaining grid connections have delayed major projects in housing and energy.

Assessing these, uncertainty is likely to be the most important factor in explaining the recent weakness, because business investment stalled specifically after 2016 when other conditions, such as record-low interest rates, were favourable. Interest rates appear less important: investment was weak even when Bank Rate was at 0.1%, consistent with evidence that firms use sticky hurdle rates. The structural services explanation accounts for part of the long-standing gap with other countries, but not for the stagnation after 2016. Overall, the low level reflects a combination of a services-heavy structure, which explains the long-run level, and policy uncertainty plus weak expected demand growth, which explain the recent stagnation. This suggests that policy stability and planning reform may do more to raise UK investment than further tax incentives.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definition of business investment and its dual role. Application: UK data (10% of GDP, G7 ranking, 2016 to 2019 stagnation, corporation tax and full expensing, services share). Analysis: four factors analysed with mechanisms (option value of waiting, capital-output ratio, accelerator vicious circle, cost of finance). Evaluation: prioritises factors using timing evidence, distinguishes long-run level from recent stagnation and draws a policy-relevant judgement, meeting the top level.

title: Government expenditure
overview: Government expenditure (G) is spending by central and local government on goods and services, around a fifth of UK GDP. This topic covers the two main influences on government spending in the specification: the trade (business) cycle, through automatic stabilisers, and discretionary fiscal policy. You need to analyse how changes in G affect AD, output and the price level, and evaluate how effective higher government spending is, which depends on spare capacity, the multiplier, crowding out, time lags and the state of the public finances.
objectives: Define government expenditure and distinguish current spending, capital spending and transfer payments.
Explain how the trade cycle affects government spending and tax revenue through automatic stabilisers.
Distinguish automatic stabilisers from discretionary fiscal policy and explain expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy.
Analyse the effect of a change in G on AD, real output and the price level using AD/AS diagrams, including a Keynesian AS curve.
Evaluate the effectiveness of government spending as a means of raising real GDP.

sections.heading: What counts as government expenditure
sections.body:
**Government expenditure** in the AD equation (G) is spending by central and local government on goods and services. It has two parts:
- **Current spending**: day-to-day spending on running public services, such as salaries of nurses, teachers and police officers, medicines and school supplies.
- **Capital spending** (public investment): spending on long-lived assets such as roads, railways, hospitals, schools, flood defences and defence equipment. In national accounts this is part of investment, but in AS questions it is usual to treat it as part of G.

**Transfer payments**, such as the state pension, Universal Credit and child benefit, are not included in G because they are not payments for goods or services produced. They redistribute income and affect AD indirectly when recipients spend them (consumption). **Debt interest** payments are also excluded from G.

This is why there are two very different measures of the size of the state:
- Total managed expenditure (all public spending including transfers and debt interest) is around 45% of UK GDP.
- G as a component of AD is only around 20% of GDP.

The largest items of UK public spending are social protection (dominated by pensions), health, education, debt interest and defence. Health spending has grown faster than GDP for decades because of an ageing population and rising costs of treatment, which puts long-term pressure on the public finances.

Government spending is financed by taxation and borrowing. The **budget deficit** is the gap between spending and revenue in a year; **public sector net debt**, the accumulated stock of borrowing, has been close to 100% of UK GDP since the pandemic. These constraints shape how much scope government has to use spending to influence the economy (4.5.3).

sections.heading: The trade cycle and automatic stabilisers
sections.body:
The **trade (business) cycle** is the fluctuation of real GDP around its long-run trend, through phases of boom, slowdown, recession and recovery (2.5.3). Government spending and taxation respond to the cycle automatically, without any new policy decision. These responses are called **automatic stabilisers**:
- **In a recession**: unemployment rises, so spending on unemployment-related benefits (such as Universal Credit) rises automatically. Incomes, profits and spending fall, so receipts from income tax, corporation tax and VAT fall. The budget deficit widens, injecting spending into the economy and cushioning the fall in AD.
- **In a boom**: unemployment falls, so benefit spending falls; incomes and spending rise, so tax receipts rise, especially from progressive income tax as more people move into higher bands. The deficit narrows, withdrawing demand and helping to restrain inflationary pressure.

Automatic stabilisers therefore make spending and taxation **counter-cyclical**: they dampen the amplitude of the cycle. Their strength depends on how progressive the tax system is and how generous the benefits system is. Countries with large welfare states, such as the Nordic countries, have stronger automatic stabilisers.

An important distinction follows. The **cyclical deficit** is the part of the deficit caused by the trade cycle, which will disappear as the economy recovers. The **structural deficit** is the deficit that would remain even if the economy were at its trend level of output, which requires discretionary action to close. After 2008 much of the UK's very large deficit was judged to be structural, which motivated austerity.

Note that some spending is **pro-cyclical**: in a boom, rising tax revenues make it tempting for governments to increase spending, adding to demand when it is least needed, while in recessions fiscal rules may force cuts at the worst time.

sections.heading: Discretionary fiscal policy
sections.body:
**Fiscal policy** is the use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence AD and the economy. **Discretionary fiscal policy** involves deliberate decisions, announced in the Budget or other fiscal events, to change spending or tax rates.
- **Expansionary (reflationary) fiscal policy**: higher G and/or lower taxes, increasing the budget deficit (or reducing a surplus) to raise AD. It is used to reduce cyclical unemployment and close a negative output gap.
- **Contractionary (deflationary) fiscal policy**: lower G and/or higher taxes to reduce AD, inflation or the deficit.

On an AD/AS diagram, an increase in G shifts AD to the right. Because G is an injection, the final shift is larger than the initial increase in spending due to the **multiplier** (2.4.4): the incomes of firms and workers who supply the government rise, they spend part of the extra income, and so on. With an MPC of 0.6 and no other leakages the multiplier would be 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 2.5; in reality taxes and imports are also leakages, so UK fiscal multipliers are much smaller.

UK examples of discretionary fiscal policy:
- **2008 to 2009**: a temporary VAT cut from 17.5% to 15% and some bringing forward of capital spending.
- **2010 to 2019**: austerity, with real cuts in many departmental budgets to reduce the structural deficit.
- **2020 to 2021**: an enormous expansion during the pandemic, including the furlough scheme, business grants and loans and NHS spending, costing hundreds of billions of pounds and pushing borrowing to around 15% of GDP in 2020 to 2021, the highest outside wartime.
- **2022 to 2023**: energy support schemes for households and firms.
- **2024 onwards**: changes to the fiscal rules to allow more borrowing for public investment, financed partly by higher employer National Insurance contributions.

Fiscal policy is also used for **supply-side** purposes: spending on education, training, infrastructure and research raises LRAS (2.6.3), which is an important evaluation point because the composition of spending matters, not just the total.

sections.heading: Does the impact depend on spare capacity?
sections.body:
The effect of an increase in G on output and prices depends on the shape of the aggregate supply curve and so on how much spare capacity exists. The **Keynesian AS curve** (see diagram) shows three ranges:
- **Horizontal range (large spare capacity)**: in a deep recession there are many unemployed workers and idle machines. An increase in G shifting AD1 to AD2 raises real output substantially (from Y1 to Y2) with almost no rise in the price level. Fiscal stimulus is very effective.
- **Intermediate range**: as output rises, bottlenecks appear in some sectors, so both output and the price level rise.
- **Vertical range (full capacity)**: an equal shift from AD3 to AD4 mainly raises the price level and output barely changes. Fiscal stimulus causes demand-pull inflation.

In the **classical (monetarist) view**, LRAS is vertical at the full employment level of output, so in the long run an increase in G cannot raise output above potential; it only raises prices or displaces private spending.

This explains why Keynesian economists supported large fiscal stimulus in 2009 and 2020, when output gaps were very negative, while others warned that continued stimulus in 2021, as the economy approached capacity, risked inflation. The size of the **output gap** at the time of the policy is therefore the single most important evaluation point in any question on fiscal expansion. The difficulty is that the output gap cannot be observed directly and estimates are frequently revised (2.5.2).

sections.heading: Limits to the effectiveness of government spending
sections.body:
Even when there is spare capacity, higher G may raise real GDP by less than hoped:
- **Crowding out.** If the government borrows to finance spending, it competes with the private sector for loanable funds, which may push up interest rates and reduce private investment and consumption. Crowding out is most likely when the economy is near full capacity and financial markets doubt the government's fiscal credibility. In a deep recession with low interest rates it is less likely; public investment can even crowd in private investment.
- **Size of the multiplier.** The UK is an open economy with significant leakages into imports and taxes, so multipliers are moderate. Estimates typically range from around 0.5 to above 1 depending on the type of spending (capital spending and transfers to low-income households tend to have larger effects) and the state of the economy.
- **Time lags.** It takes time to recognise a problem, decide on a policy, pass legislation and actually spend the money. Infrastructure projects take years. By the time spending happens, the economy may have recovered, making it pro-cyclical.
- **Ricardian equivalence and confidence.** If households expect today's borrowing to mean higher taxes in future, they may save more, offsetting the stimulus. Conversely, if markets lose confidence in public finances, gilt yields rise sharply, as in September 2022 after the unfunded tax cuts in the mini-budget, raising borrowing costs across the economy.
- **Debt sustainability.** With public sector net debt close to 100% of GDP and debt interest over £100bn a year, the UK has less fiscal space than before 2008. Fiscal rules monitored by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) limit how much the government can borrow.
- **Government failure.** Spending may be poorly targeted, subject to cost overruns (as with HS2) or influenced by political rather than economic priorities.

The overall effectiveness of higher G therefore depends on the output gap, how the spending is financed, what it is spent on, how quickly it can be delivered and the credibility of the government's fiscal framework.

Government spending on day-to-day running of public services, such as wages and supplies.
Government spending on long-lived assets such as roads, schools and hospitals.
The use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence aggregate demand and the economy.

The part of the budget deficit that would remain if the economy were at its trend level of output.
The part of the budget deficit caused by the trade cycle, which disappears as the economy recovers.

The fluctuation of real GDP around its long-run trend through phases of boom, slowdown, recession and recovery.

diagrams.title: Fiscal stimulus and the Keynesian AS curve
diagrams.caption: With large spare capacity, an increase in G from AD1 to AD2 raises real output from Y1 to Y2 with almost no rise in the price level. Near full capacity an equal shift from AD3 to AD4 raises output only from Y3 to Y4 but pushes the price level up sharply.

diagrams.title: The trade cycle and automatic stabilisers
diagrams.caption: Real GDP fluctuates around its trend. In a recession benefit spending rises and tax receipts fall automatically, adding to AD; in a boom the reverse happens. Automatic stabilisers reduce the amplitude of the cycle.

diagrams.title: Increase in government spending
diagrams.caption: An increase in G (plus multiplier effects) shifts AD from AD1 to AD2. Real output rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level from P1 to P2. The split between output and inflation depends on the slope of SRAS.

formulae.name: Budget balance
formulae.formula: Tax revenue - government spending (negative = deficit)

formulae.name: Simple multiplier
formulae.formula: 1 / (1 - MPC) or 1 / MPW where MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM
formulae.example: MPS 0.1, MPT 0.3, MPM 0.3: multiplier = 1 / 0.7 = 1.43, so £10bn extra G raises GDP by about £14.3bn.

applications: During the pandemic the UK government spent hundreds of billions of pounds on the furlough scheme, business support and the NHS. Borrowing rose to around 15% of GDP in 2020 to 2021. Output still fell by around 10% in 2020 because of lockdowns, but the support prevented mass unemployment and allowed a rapid rebound in 2021.

Austerity from 2010 cut departmental spending in real terms, especially in local government, justice and welfare. Critics argue it slowed the recovery when the output gap was negative and interest rates were at their lower bound; supporters argue it restored fiscal credibility and kept gilt yields low.

The September 2022 mini-budget announced large unfunded tax cuts without an OBR forecast. Gilt yields rose sharply, sterling fell to a record low against the dollar and the Bank of England intervened to stabilise pension funds, demonstrating that fiscal credibility constrains discretionary policy.

From 2024 the UK changed its fiscal rules to target public sector net financial liabilities rather than net debt, creating more room to borrow for investment. The aim is to raise public investment, which had been low by international standards, while balancing the current budget.

In the USA, very large fiscal packages in 2020 to 2021 boosted demand strongly and are widely seen as contributing to higher US inflation in 2021 to 2022, an example of stimulus applied as the economy approached the vertical range of AS.
evaluation: The output gap is decisive: with a large negative output gap, higher G raises real output with little inflation; near full capacity it mainly raises prices, as the Keynesian AS curve shows.
Composition matters: capital spending on infrastructure, skills and research can raise LRAS as well as AD, whereas current spending mainly affects demand.

Financing matters: borrowing may crowd out private investment if interest rates rise, while tax-financed spending has a smaller net effect on AD (though a balanced budget multiplier is still positive).
Time lags can make discretionary policy pro-cyclical; automatic stabilisers avoid this problem because they respond immediately.
Fiscal space is limited: with debt near 100% of GDP and debt interest over £100bn a year, the opportunity cost of borrowing is high and market confidence must be maintained.

The size of the multiplier is uncertain and depends on leakages, the state of the economy and the response of monetary policy; if the Bank of England raises interest rates in response, the stimulus may be offset.
misconceptions: Including pensions and benefits in G. They are transfers; they affect AD only through consumption.
Confusing the budget deficit (a flow in one year) with the national debt (the accumulated stock).
Assuming more government spending always increases real GDP. Near full capacity, it mainly causes inflation; it may also crowd out private spending.
Thinking automatic stabilisers require new decisions. They operate through the existing tax and benefit system without any change in policy.
Showing an increase in G as a shift of SRAS. It shifts AD; only spending that raises productive capacity shifts LRAS, and that takes time.
exam_tips: Use the Keynesian AS curve when evaluating fiscal stimulus: show equal AD shifts in the horizontal and vertical ranges to demonstrate how the impact depends on spare capacity.
Always distinguish automatic stabilisers from discretionary policy; it is a frequent Section A and data-response question.

In 25-mark essays, structure your evaluation around the output gap, the multiplier, crowding out, time lags, the composition of spending and fiscal credibility, and reach a judgement for the specific UK context.
Quote UK fiscal facts accurately: G around 20% of GDP, total spending around 45%, debt close to 100% of GDP, the role of the OBR.
Synoptic links: the multiplier (2.4.4), output gaps (2.5.2), demand-side policy (2.6.2), public expenditure and public sector finances (4.5.1, 4.5.3).

model_answer.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of an increase in government expenditure as a means of increasing real GDP in the UK. (25 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Government expenditure is spending by central and local government on goods and services, such as NHS staff, schools and infrastructure. It is around a fifth of UK GDP and is a component of aggregate demand: AD = C + I + G + (X - M). Real GDP is the value of output adjusted for inflation. An increase in G is a form of expansionary discretionary fiscal policy.

The direct effect of an increase in G is to shift AD to the right from AD1 to AD2. If the government spends an extra £20bn on building hospitals and new railway lines, construction firms receive extra revenue and hire more workers, so real output rises from Y1 to Y2. The effect is magnified by the multiplier: construction workers spend part of their extra income on goods and services, raising the incomes of other firms and workers, who spend part of theirs, and so on. If the marginal propensity to withdraw (saving, taxation and imports) is 0.6, the multiplier is 1 / 0.6 = 1.67, so the £20bn injection would eventually raise real GDP by around £33bn. Higher sales and confidence may also encourage firms to invest to expand capacity through the accelerator, adding further to AD.

Moreover, some government spending raises the economy's productive capacity. Capital spending on transport, energy networks and digital infrastructure lowers firms' costs and raises productivity, while spending on education, training and healthcare improves the quality and quantity of labour. Over time these shift LRAS to the right, allowing real GDP to grow without inflation. This is particularly relevant to the UK, where public investment has been low by international standards and weak productivity growth of only around 0.5% a year since 2008 has held back living standards.

However, the effectiveness of higher G depends critically on the amount of spare capacity in the economy. Using a Keynesian AS curve, if the economy is in a deep recession with a large negative output gap, an increase in AD raises real output substantially with almost no rise in the price level, as there are unemployed workers and idle machines available. This was the situation in 2009 and 2020. But if the economy is close to full capacity, an equal increase in AD mainly raises the price level. In the classical view, LRAS is vertical, so in the long run higher G cannot raise real GDP beyond potential at all; it simply causes demand-pull inflation. In 2023 to 2024 the UK was estimated to have only a small negative output gap and inflation was well above target, so a large demand stimulus would have mainly added to inflation and probably led the Bank of England to keep interest rates higher for longer, offsetting the effect on output.

A second limitation is crowding out. Higher G financed by borrowing increases the government's demand for loanable funds, which can push up long-term interest rates. This raises the cost of borrowing for firms and households, reducing investment and consumption. The risk is higher when public sector net debt is already close to 100% of GDP, as in the UK. The reaction of financial markets to the unfunded mini-budget in September 2022, when gilt yields rose sharply and mortgage rates jumped, shows that fiscal expansion without credibility can reduce private spending substantially. In contrast, if the spending is financed by higher taxes, the net effect on AD is smaller, though the balanced budget multiplier is still positive because some of the tax would otherwise have been saved.

Third, the size of the multiplier in the UK is uncertain and probably modest. The UK is an open economy with a high marginal propensity to import, so part of the extra spending leaks abroad, and taxes take a further share at each round. Estimates of UK fiscal multipliers generally lie between around 0.5 and just above 1, depending on the type of spending and the state of the economy. Spending on infrastructure tends to have a larger multiplier than transfers to high-income households.

Fourth, time lags reduce effectiveness. Large infrastructure projects take years to plan and build, as the history of HS2 shows, with long delays and large cost overruns. By the time spending peaks, the economy may already be recovering, making the policy pro-cyclical. Government failure, through poor project selection or political priorities, may also mean spending does not go where it raises output most.

Weighing these arguments, an increase in government expenditure is most effective at raising real GDP when three conditions hold: there is a significant negative output gap, the spending is on productive investment that raises LRAS as well as AD, and it is financed in a credible way that does not trigger a sharp rise in interest rates. In 2020 these conditions were largely met, and fiscal support prevented a much deeper and longer recession. In the current UK context, with limited spare capacity, inflation above target and high debt, a general increase in current spending would be less effective, raising prices and debt interest costs more than real output. The most effective approach would be a targeted, credible increase in public investment in areas such as energy infrastructure, planning capacity and skills, where the long-run supply-side benefits are greatest. Therefore, government spending can increase real GDP, but its effectiveness depends far more on what it is spent on and when than on the amount.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate definitions of G, real GDP and expansionary fiscal policy, plus the AD equation. Application: UK-specific evidence (2009 and 2020, output gap in 2023 to 2024, debt near 100% of GDP, the mini-budget, HS2, productivity data). Analysis: full chains through the multiplier (with a calculation), the accelerator and LRAS, plus a Keynesian AS analysis. Evaluation: considers spare capacity, crowding out, multiplier size and time lags, weighs them against the UK context and reaches a conditional, well-supported judgement, meeting Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

title: Net trade
overview: Net trade (X - M) is the value of exports minus the value of imports and is the component of aggregate demand that connects the UK to the world economy. Although net trade is a small share of UK GDP, exports and imports are each around 30% of GDP, so changes in either have large effects on AD. This topic covers the main influences on net trade in the specification: real income (at home and abroad), exchange rates, the state of the world economy, the degree of protectionism and non-price factors.
objectives: Define exports, imports and net trade and explain why imports are subtracted from AD.
Analyse how changes in domestic and foreign real income affect imports and exports.
Explain and calculate how exchange rate changes affect the prices of exports and imports.
Analyse the effects of the state of the world economy, protectionism and non-price factors on net trade.
Evaluate how far changes in net trade affect UK AD, using the Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve.

sections.heading: Net trade as a component of AD
sections.body:
**Exports (X)** are goods and services produced in the UK and sold to non-residents. They are an **injection** into the circular flow: foreign spending that creates UK output and incomes. **Imports (M)** are goods and services produced abroad and bought by UK residents. They are a **withdrawal**: spending by UK residents that creates incomes abroad rather than in the UK.

**Net trade** = X - M. Imports are subtracted in the AD equation because consumption, investment and government spending all include some spending on imported goods and services, which must be removed to measure spending on UK output.

The UK is an **open economy**: exports and imports of goods and services are each around 30% of GDP. Net trade is usually small and negative, so it is easy to underestimate its importance. But because the gross flows are large, a modest percentage change in exports or imports causes a significant shift in AD. A 5% fall in exports, for example, is a fall of around 1.5% of GDP before multiplier effects.

Net trade differs from the **current account** (2.1.4): net trade covers only trade in goods and services, while the current account also includes primary and secondary income.

The determinants of net trade fall into five groups: real income at home and abroad, the exchange rate, the state of the world economy, protectionism and non-price competitiveness. In an exam answer, always state which side of the account is affected (exports, imports or both) and the direction of the effect on AD.

sections.heading: Real income at home and abroad
sections.body:
**Domestic real income** mainly affects **imports**. When UK real incomes rise, households spend more on all goods, including imported ones: cars, electronics, clothing, foreign holidays. Firms import more raw materials and components to meet higher demand. Many imports are **income elastic**: the **marginal propensity to import** (MPM) measures the share of each extra pound of income spent on imports. If UK income rises £10bn and imports rise £3bn, MPM = 0.3. So during a UK boom imports rise strongly and net trade tends to worsen; in a UK recession imports fall and net trade tends to improve, even though this improvement reflects weakness rather than strength.

**Foreign real income** mainly affects **exports**. When incomes in the UK's trading partners rise, they buy more UK goods and services: Scotch whisky, cars, pharmaceuticals, financial and legal services, and university places. The EU is the UK's largest trading partner, taking roughly 40% of UK exports, and the USA is the largest single-country export market. Growth in these economies is therefore a major determinant of UK export demand.

**Relative growth rates** therefore matter. If the UK grows faster than its trading partners, imports grow faster than exports, and net trade deteriorates. This is one reason why the UK, which has often grown faster than the euro area since 2010, has run trade deficits.

The **composition** of trade also matters. Demand for luxury and high-value services exports tends to be highly income elastic, so UK exports of these services rise strongly when world incomes grow, while exports of primary commodities by developing countries have low income elasticity, which limits their gains from world growth.

sections.heading: Exchange rates
sections.body:
The **exchange rate** is the price of one currency in terms of another, for example £1 = $1.25. A change in the exchange rate changes the relative prices of exports and imports.

A **depreciation** (fall in the value of the pound):
- Makes UK exports **cheaper** in foreign currency, so foreign demand for them should rise.
- Makes imports **more expensive** in pounds, so UK demand for them should fall.
- So net trade should improve and AD shift right.

An **appreciation** has the opposite effects. A useful memory aid is SPICED: **S**trong **P**ound, **I**mports **C**heap, **E**xports **D**ear.

**Worked example.** A UK car sells for £20,000.
- At £1 = $1.30, its US price is 20,000 x 1.30 = $26,000.
- If the pound depreciates to £1 = $1.20, its US price falls to 20,000 x 1.20 = $24,000, a fall of 7.7%.
- A US machine priced at $100,000 costs 100,000 / 1.30 = £76,923 before the depreciation and 100,000 / 1.20 = £83,333 after, a rise of 8.3%.

**Will net trade actually improve?** That depends on the **price elasticities of demand** for exports and imports. The **Marshall-Lerner condition** states that a depreciation improves the trade balance only if the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than 1 (in absolute value). In the short run demand is often inelastic, because contracts are fixed, buyers take time to find alternatives and firms take time to expand. The trade balance may therefore worsen at first before improving: the **J-curve** effect.

The exchange rate itself is determined by the supply and demand for the currency (see diagram). Lower UK interest rates, falling investor confidence or a widening current account deficit increase the supply of pounds on currency markets and push the exchange rate down. A depreciation also has a cost: higher import prices raise firms' costs and consumer prices, causing cost-push inflation (2.1.2), which erodes the competitive gain over time.

sections.heading: The world economy, protectionism and non-price factors
sections.body:
**The state of the world economy.** A global recession reduces demand for UK exports, while a global boom raises it. Global shocks also affect prices: higher world energy prices raise the value of UK energy imports. Globalisation has made trade more sensitive to world conditions, because production is organised in **global value chains**: a slowdown in Germany's car industry, for example, reduces demand for UK-made components. The 2008 to 2009 global financial crisis caused world trade volumes to fall by more than 10% in 2009, much faster than world GDP.

**Protectionism** is the use of barriers to protect domestic producers from foreign competition:
- **Tariffs** (taxes on imports) raise import prices and reduce import volumes.
- **Quotas** limit the quantity of imports.
- **Non-tariff barriers** such as regulations, product standards, customs checks and rules of origin raise the cost of trading.
- **Subsidies** to domestic producers make them more competitive.

Protectionism by **other countries** reduces UK exports; protectionism by the **UK** may reduce imports but invites retaliation. Leaving the EU single market and customs union in 2021 created non-tariff barriers for UK-EU trade, which most studies find has reduced UK goods trade with the EU, particularly for small firms. In 2025 the USA introduced a baseline 10% tariff on most imports, including from the UK, and higher tariffs on some sectors; a UK-US agreement in 2025 reduced tariffs on a quota of UK car exports, but the episode increased uncertainty for exporters.

**Non-price factors** determine competitiveness as much as prices do: product quality, design, reliability, brand reputation, after-sales service, delivery times and innovation. Many UK exports, such as financial services, pharmaceuticals, aerospace engines and luxury cars, compete mainly on quality and reputation, so their demand is relatively price inelastic. Improving non-price competitiveness depends on investment, research and development, and skills, which links net trade to the supply side of the economy.

sections.heading: The macroeconomic effect of changes in net trade
sections.body:
An increase in net trade (higher exports or lower imports) shifts AD to the right, raising real output and employment in export industries and import-competing industries, and through the multiplier in the wider economy. A fall shifts AD to the left.

Evaluating the size of the effect requires several judgements:
- **Size of the change relative to GDP**: a change in exports to a small market has little effect; a recession in the EU or USA has a large one.
- **Elasticities**: the more price elastic demand for exports and imports, the larger the effect of exchange rate changes.
- **Time period**: trade volumes adjust slowly (J-curve), and firms need time to enter new markets.
- **Import content of exports**: many UK exports contain imported components, so a depreciation raises their costs too, reducing the net benefit.
- **Supply capacity**: if UK firms are close to capacity, they cannot expand exports quickly in response to higher demand.
- **Offsetting changes**: a depreciation that raises net exports also raises inflation, which may prompt the Bank of England to raise interest rates, reducing C and I.

Strategies to improve net trade in the long run are supply-side: raising productivity, investing in skills and infrastructure, and agreeing trade deals that reduce barriers. Relying on depreciation alone tends to deliver a temporary gain at the cost of higher inflation and lower real incomes, as the UK experience after 2016 suggests.

key_terms.definition: Goods and services produced domestically and sold to non-residents; an injection into the circular flow.
Goods and services produced abroad and bought by domestic residents; a withdrawal from the circular flow.
The value of exports minus the value of imports (X - M).
The proportion of an additional unit of income spent on imports: ΔM / ΔY.
The price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.
A fall in the value of a floating currency relative to other currencies.
A rise in the value of a floating currency relative to other currencies.
A depreciation improves the trade balance only if the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds 1.
The tendency for the trade balance to worsen in the short run after a depreciation before improving as volumes adjust.
Policies that restrict imports or support domestic producers, such as tariffs, quotas, non-tariff barriers and subsidies.
The ability to sell goods abroad because of quality, design, reliability, brand and service rather than price.

diagrams.title: Depreciation of sterling
diagrams.caption: If UK residents and investors sell more pounds (for example after a cut in UK interest rates or a loss of confidence), the supply of £ shifts right from S£1 to S£2. The exchange rate falls from ER1 to ER2, making UK exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer in pounds.

diagrams.title: A global slowdown reduces net trade and AD
diagrams.caption: A recession in major trading partners or new foreign tariffs reduce UK exports, so net trade falls and AD shifts left from AD1 to AD2. Real output falls from Y1 to Y2, with multiplier effects on employment beyond the export sector.

formulae.name: Net trade
formulae.formula: X - M

formulae.name: Foreign currency price of an export
formulae.formula: Sterling price x exchange rate (foreign currency per £)

formulae.name: Sterling price of an import
formulae.formula: Foreign currency price / exchange rate

formulae.name: Marginal propensity to import
formulae.formula: MPM = ΔM / ΔY

formulae.name: Marshall-Lerner condition
formulae.formula: |PEDx| + |PEDm| > 1
formulae.example: PEDx = -0.4 and PEDm = -0.3: sum 0.7 < 1, so a depreciation initially worsens the trade balance.

applications: After the 2016 EU referendum, sterling fell sharply against the dollar and euro. UK exporters became more price competitive, but import prices rose and CPI inflation reached around 3% in 2017. The improvement in net trade was modest, consistent with low short-run elasticities and the high import content of many UK exports.

Since the UK left the EU single market and customs union in 2021, exporters have faced customs declarations, rules of origin and regulatory checks. Studies by the OBR and others suggest UK trade intensity is lower than it would otherwise have been, with small firms most affected.

In 2025 the USA imposed a baseline 10% tariff on imports from most countries, including the UK, with higher rates for some sectors and countries. A UK-US deal reduced tariffs on a quota of UK car exports, illustrating how protectionism and trade negotiations directly affect UK net trade.

The UK exports a large volume of services, especially financial, professional and business services, which compete mainly on expertise and reputation. This non-price competitiveness means UK services exports respond more to world income than to exchange rate changes.

China's rapid export growth in electric vehicles, batteries and solar panels has prompted tariffs from the USA and EU, showing that protectionism can shift trade flows between countries and that UK markets may receive diverted Chinese goods.
evaluation: The Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve mean a depreciation may worsen net trade in the short run; the long-run outcome depends on elasticities.
A depreciation raises import prices and inflation, eroding competitiveness over time and possibly prompting higher interest rates that offset the gain in AD.
The importance of trading partners varies: a slowdown in the EU or USA matters far more for the UK than one in a small market.
Non-price factors may dominate price factors for UK exports such as services, pharmaceuticals and aerospace, so exchange rate changes have limited effects.
Supply constraints limit the response: firms near capacity or lacking skilled workers cannot quickly increase exports.
Protectionism invites retaliation and raises costs for firms that rely on imported inputs, so its net effect on net trade and AD may be negative.
misconceptions: Saying a strong pound makes exports cheaper. An appreciation makes exports more expensive in foreign currency and imports cheaper (SPICED).
Assuming a depreciation always improves the trade balance immediately. It depends on elasticities; the J-curve shows it often worsens first.
Thinking that a rise in UK incomes increases exports. Rising UK incomes mainly raise imports; foreign incomes drive exports.
Treating net trade and the current account as identical. The current account also includes primary and secondary income.
Arguing that a fall in imports during a recession shows the economy is healthier. Net trade improves because UK demand is weak.
exam_tips: Exchange rate calculations appear frequently in Section A: multiply the sterling price by the exchange rate to get the foreign currency price, divide a foreign price by the exchange rate to get the sterling price, and calculate percentage changes carefully.
When analysing a change in the exchange rate, state the effect on export prices, import prices, volumes, net trade, AD and then on inflation, and evaluate with Marshall-Lerner and the J-curve.
Distinguish clearly between factors that affect exports (foreign income, foreign protectionism) and those that affect imports (domestic income, domestic tariffs).
Use specific UK examples: sterling after 2016, post-Brexit trade barriers, US tariffs in 2025, the services surplus.
Synoptic links: balance of payments (2.1.4, 4.1.7), exchange rates (4.1.8), international competitiveness (4.1.9), protectionism (4.1.6) and globalisation (4.1.1).

model_answer.question: Assess the likely impact of a significant depreciation of sterling on UK net trade and aggregate demand. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
A depreciation is a fall in the value of the pound against other currencies on the foreign exchange market. It could result from a cut in UK interest rates relative to other countries, or a fall in investor confidence, which increases the supply of pounds and lowers the exchange rate. Net trade is the value of exports minus the value of imports and is a component of aggregate demand.

A depreciation makes UK exports cheaper in foreign currency. For example, a £20,000 car exported to the USA would fall from $26,000 to $24,000 if the exchange rate fell from $1.30 to $1.20, a price cut of 7.7%. If demand is price elastic, US buyers buy more UK cars, raising the volume and value of UK exports. At the same time, imports become more expensive in pounds: a $100,000 machine would rise from £76,923 to £83,333. UK firms and households switch to domestically produced substitutes, so import volumes fall. With higher exports and lower imports, net trade improves and AD shifts to the right. Through the multiplier, higher incomes in export and import-competing industries are spent, raising real output and employment more widely.

However, the size and timing of the effect depend on price elasticities. The Marshall-Lerner condition states that a depreciation improves the trade balance only if the combined price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceed one. In the short run, demand is often inelastic, because contracts are fixed and buyers take time to switch suppliers, so the higher sterling cost of imports outweighs the rise in export volumes. Net trade may therefore initially worsen, the J-curve effect, and only improve after one or two years.

In addition, many UK exports compete on non-price factors. Financial services, pharmaceuticals and aerospace engines are bought for their quality and reputation, so demand is relatively price inelastic and a depreciation does little to raise sales. Many UK exports also have a high import content: a car assembled in the UK uses imported components, whose costs rise after a depreciation, reducing the price advantage. The depreciation also raises import prices for consumers, causing cost-push inflation; after 2016, CPI rose to around 3%, squeezing real incomes and consumption, which offsets part of the rise in AD. If inflation rises above target, the Bank of England may raise interest rates, reducing consumption and investment further.

Overall, a significant depreciation is likely to improve UK net trade and AD, but by less than a simple analysis suggests and only after a time lag. The gain will be largest for price-sensitive manufactured exports to markets with growing incomes, and smallest for services. Since higher inflation erodes the competitive gain over time, a lasting improvement in net trade is more likely to come from raising non-price competitiveness through investment and productivity than from a weaker currency.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: definitions of depreciation and net trade and the mechanism linking them. Application: numerical illustration of export and import price changes and UK evidence from 2016. Analysis: a full chain from exchange rate to prices, volumes, net trade, AD and the multiplier. Evaluation: Marshall-Lerner, the J-curve, non-price competitiveness, import content, inflation and the monetary policy response, leading to a supported and qualified judgement that reaches the top level for a 12-mark question.

check.q: The exchange rate changes from £1 = €1.20 to £1 = €1.10. What happens to the euro price of a UK export priced at £50?
options: Rises from €55 to €60
Falls from €60 to €55
Falls from €50 to €45
Stays at €50
check.explanation: At €1.20 the price is 50 x 1.20 = €60; at €1.10 it is 50 x 1.10 = €55. The pound has depreciated, making UK exports cheaper in euros.

check.q: Which of the following is most likely to increase UK exports?
options: Rise in UK real incomes
Appreciation of sterling
Faster economic growth in the euro area
New tariffs imposed by the USA on UK goods
check.explanation: Higher incomes in the UK's largest trading partner raise demand for UK exports. A raises imports, B makes exports dearer and D reduces exports.

check.q: The price elasticity of demand for UK exports is -0.3 and for UK imports is -0.4. According to the Marshall-Lerner condition, a depreciation will:
options: Improve the trade balance immediately
Worsen the trade balance
Have no effect on the trade balance
Always cause a trade surplus

They are subject to high UK tariffs
Their price is set in pounds abroad
