title: Characteristics of AS
overview: Aggregate supply (AS) is the total quantity of real output that firms in an economy plan to produce at each price level. This topic introduces the two AS curves you will use throughout Themes 2 and 4: short-run aggregate supply (SRAS), which slopes upwards because some costs are fixed in the short run, and long-run aggregate supply (LRAS), which reflects the economy's productive capacity. You must be able to distinguish a movement along the SRAS curve from a shift, and to explain how SRAS and LRAS relate to each other.
objectives: Define aggregate supply and distinguish the short run from the long run in macroeconomics.
Explain why the SRAS curve slopes upwards.
Distinguish a movement along SRAS (caused by a change in the price level) from a shift in SRAS (caused by a change in costs).
Explain what LRAS represents and why the classical LRAS is vertical.
Show the relationship between AD, SRAS and LRAS, including long-run adjustment to full employment.

sections.heading: What aggregate supply is
sections.body:
**Aggregate supply** is the total planned output of goods and services that all firms in an economy are willing and able to produce at each possible price level over a given period. Like AD, it is drawn against the **price level** on the vertical axis and **real output** (real GDP) on the horizontal axis.

Macroeconomists distinguish two time periods:
- The **short run** is a period in which the prices of some factors of production, particularly money wages, are fixed, and the quantity and quality of factors of production (the productive capacity of the economy) are given.
- The **long run** is a period long enough for all factor prices, including wages, to adjust fully, and in which productive capacity can change through investment, technology, education and changes in the labour force.

This gives two curves:
- **Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS)** shows how much output firms supply at each price level when input costs such as money wages are fixed.
- **Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS)** shows the maximum output the economy can produce when all resources are fully and efficiently employed: its **productive potential**, equivalent to a point on the production possibility frontier.

SRAS is about the use of existing capacity in response to changing prices and costs; LRAS is about the size of that capacity. Keep this distinction in mind: it determines which curve shifts in response to any given event.

sections.heading: Why SRAS slopes upwards
sections.body:
The SRAS curve slopes upwards: at a higher price level firms are willing to supply more real output. There are two main reasons.

**1. Fixed input costs and profitability.** In the short run, many costs are fixed in money terms: wages are set in contracts for a year at a time, rents are fixed by leases and some raw materials are bought on forward contracts. If the price level rises while these costs stay the same, the gap between the price firms receive and their costs widens. Production becomes more profitable, so firms expand output. Conversely, a fall in the price level with sticky costs squeezes profit margins, so firms cut output.

**2. Rising marginal costs as output rises.** As firms increase output using their existing capital, they move up their marginal cost curves. They must pay overtime premiums, hire less experienced workers, use older and less efficient machinery and pay more for scarce inputs. The law of diminishing returns means each extra unit costs more to produce. Firms will only supply this extra output if the price they receive rises to cover the higher costs.

The SRAS curve becomes **steeper as the economy approaches full capacity**: when there is lots of spare capacity firms can raise output without much increase in costs, but near full capacity bottlenecks and labour shortages mean large increases in cost and price for small increases in output.

Remember that SRAS is not simply the sum of firms' supply curves in microeconomics. A firm's supply curve depends on its own price relative to other prices; SRAS concerns the general price level relative to input costs.

sections.heading: Movements along vs shifts of SRAS
sections.body:
The distinction follows the same logic as in microeconomics.

**A movement along SRAS** is caused by a change in the **price level**, which itself is usually caused by a shift in AD. When AD increases from AD1 to AD2, the price level rises and firms respond by supplying more output: the economy moves up along the existing SRAS curve, from E1 to E2 on the demand-pull diagram in 2.1.2. Nothing has happened to firms' costs at each level of output.

**A shift of SRAS** is caused by a change in **costs of production** (or anything else that changes the output firms will supply at every price level):
- **Leftward shift (decrease in SRAS)**: higher costs of raw materials and energy, higher money wages not matched by productivity, a depreciation that raises import prices, higher indirect taxes or employer National Insurance contributions, new regulations that raise costs, or supply shocks such as a poor harvest or disruption to supply chains.
- **Rightward shift (increase in SRAS)**: lower commodity and energy prices, an appreciation of the currency, lower business taxes, subsidies, or short-run improvements in productivity.

The determinants are developed in 2.3.2. An SRAS shift to the right lowers the price level and raises real output, which is the ideal combination; a shift to the left creates **stagflation**, with rising prices and falling output.

A key exam skill is identifying correctly whether an event affects AD (spending) or SRAS (costs). Some events affect both: a depreciation raises net exports (AD right) and import costs (SRAS left), and a rise in the National Living Wage raises firms' costs (SRAS left) and the incomes of low-paid workers (AD right).

sections.heading: Long-run aggregate supply
sections.body:
**LRAS** represents the productive potential of the economy: the level of real output that can be produced when all factors of production are fully and efficiently employed. It is determined by the **quantity and quality of factors of production** (labour, capital, land and enterprise) and by the **state of technology** and institutions.

In the **classical (free-market) view**, the LRAS curve is **vertical** at the full-employment level of output (Yfe), also called potential output. The reasoning is that in the long run all prices and wages are flexible. If the price level rises, money wages and other costs rise in proportion, so real wages and the profitability of production are unchanged, and firms do not want to supply more output. The level of output in the long run therefore depends only on productive capacity, not on the price level or AD.

Factors that shift LRAS to the right include:
- More or better capital through investment.
- Improvements in technology and productivity.
- Better education, training and health of the workforce (human capital).
- A larger labour force through migration, higher participation or a growing population.
- Supply-side policies such as deregulation or competition policy that improve efficiency.

LRAS shifts left if capacity is lost, for example through a long recession that causes hysteresis, war, natural disasters, the closure of industries or a fall in the size of the labour force.

The **Keynesian** view of LRAS, which is horizontal at low output, then curves upwards and becomes vertical at full capacity, is developed in 2.3.3. Both views agree that there is a maximum level of output, shown by the vertical section.

sections.heading: How AD, SRAS and LRAS fit together
sections.body:
In **long-run equilibrium** AD, SRAS and LRAS all intersect at the same point: the economy is producing at full capacity (Yfe) and there is no output gap.

**Short-run equilibrium** can differ from the long run. Suppose AD increases from AD1 to AD2. In the short run, with money wages fixed, the economy moves along SRAS1 to E2: real output rises above Yfe (a **positive output gap**) and the price level rises. Firms produce beyond normal capacity by using overtime and running machines harder.

The classical view says this is temporary. Workers notice that prices have risen, so their real wages have fallen. When contracts are renegotiated they demand higher money wages. Firms' costs rise, so SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2. This continues until output returns to Yfe at E3, at a permanently higher price level. The long-run result of the increase in AD is therefore only inflation, with no lasting increase in output.

The reverse happens after a fall in AD: output falls below Yfe (a negative output gap) and unemployment rises. Classical economists argue that wages and prices then fall, shifting SRAS right until full employment is restored. Keynesians counter that wages are sticky downwards, so this adjustment may take a very long time, and that, as Keynes put it, in the long run we are all dead. This disagreement about how quickly the economy self-corrects is the root of the debate about whether governments should actively manage AD.

Note also that the economy's position relative to LRAS can be shown on a PPF: output below Yfe is a point inside the PPF, and an outward shift of the PPF corresponds to a rightward shift of LRAS.

key_terms.definition: The total planned output of goods and services that firms are willing and able to produce at each price level over a given period.
The total output firms will supply at each price level when some input costs, especially money wages, are fixed.
The productive potential of the economy: the output that can be produced when all factors are fully and efficiently employed.
A period in which some factor prices, especially money wages, are fixed and productive capacity is given.
A period long enough for all factor prices to adjust fully and for productive capacity to change.
The level of real output produced when all factors of production are fully employed; also called potential output.
An unexpected event that changes costs of production and shifts SRAS, such as a sharp rise in energy prices.
Rising inflation combined with falling or stagnant output and rising unemployment, usually caused by a leftward shift of SRAS.
The maximum output an economy can produce with its existing resources and technology.

diagrams.title: Movement along SRAS
diagrams.caption: A rise in the price level from P1 to P2 (usually caused by higher AD), with input costs fixed, makes production more profitable, so firms increase real output from Y1 to Y2: a movement along SRAS from A to B.

diagrams.title: Shifts in SRAS
diagrams.caption: Lower costs (for example cheaper energy) shift SRAS right to SRAS2: the price level falls to P2 and real output rises to Y2. Higher costs shift SRAS left to SRAS3: the price level rises to P3 while output falls to Y3 (stagflation).

diagrams.title: Long-run equilibrium
diagrams.caption: In long-run equilibrium AD, SRAS and the classical vertical LRAS intersect at full-employment output Yfe. There is no output gap.

diagrams.title: Classical long-run adjustment to higher AD
diagrams.caption: Higher AD moves the economy from E1 to E2: output rises above Yfe in the short run. As money wages rise to restore real wages, SRAS shifts left to SRAS2 and the economy returns to Yfe at E3 with a higher price level P3.

applications: The 2022 energy price shock was a classic leftward shift in SRAS: wholesale gas prices rose several-fold after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, raising costs across the UK economy. CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022 while output stagnated, the stagflation outcome predicted by the AD/AS model.

The fall in oil prices from over $100 a barrel in 2014 to below $40 in early 2016 was a positive supply shock for oil importers such as the UK. SRAS shifted right, contributing to near-zero CPI inflation in 2015 while growth continued.

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates the UK's potential output and the output gap in each forecast. Its judgement that the UK's potential growth rate has fallen since 2008, mainly because of weak productivity growth, is equivalent to saying that LRAS has been shifting right much more slowly than before.

After the pandemic, many economies found that potential output had been damaged by labour shortages, higher inactivity and supply chain disruption. In the UK, the rise in inactivity due to long-term sickness reduced the size of the labour force, slowing the rightward shift of LRAS.
evaluation: The speed of long-run adjustment is disputed: classical economists expect wages to adjust quickly, while Keynesians argue wages are sticky, especially downwards, so the economy may stay below full employment for years.
The slope of SRAS varies with spare capacity: when the economy is near full capacity, SRAS is steep and AD shifts mainly affect prices; with large spare capacity it is flatter.
Many real-world events shift more than one curve: a depreciation, a minimum wage rise or a tax change can affect AD and SRAS simultaneously, so the net effect on prices and output is ambiguous.
Potential output (LRAS) cannot be observed directly; estimates are uncertain and revised, so judging whether the economy is above or below LRAS is difficult in practice.
Supply shocks may be temporary (a short-lived spike in oil prices) or persistent; their effect on inflation depends on whether they trigger second-round wage increases.
misconceptions: Shifting SRAS when the price level changes. A change in the price level causes a movement along SRAS; only changes in costs shift it.
Drawing LRAS as upward sloping. The classical LRAS is vertical at Yfe; the Keynesian LRAS is horizontal, then curved, then vertical.
Confusing SRAS and LRAS shifts. A rise in oil prices shifts SRAS; an improvement in education shifts LRAS. If productive capacity changes, LRAS shifts.
Thinking output can never exceed LRAS. In the short run the economy can produce beyond normal capacity (a positive output gap) by using overtime and running machines harder.
Assuming an increase in AD raises output permanently. In the classical model, output returns to Yfe and only the price level is higher in the long run.
exam_tips: Label the axes price level and real output, label every curve (AD1, SRAS1, LRAS) and mark equilibria with dotted guides to both axes. Examiners award diagram marks for accuracy.
When an event occurs, ask: does it change spending (AD), costs (SRAS) or capacity (LRAS)? State your answer explicitly before drawing.
Section A short-answer questions often ask why SRAS slopes upwards or what causes a shift: use fixed costs and rising marginal costs for the slope, and give specific cost examples for shifts.
Use the classical adjustment diagram to evaluate demand-side policy: it shows why a permanent stimulus may only raise prices in the long run.
Synoptic links: inflation (2.1.2), output gaps (2.5.2), the PPF (1.1.4) and supply-side policy (2.6.3).

model_answer.question: Examine the likely effects of a large fall in global oil prices on the UK economy. Use an AD/AS diagram to support your answer. (10 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Oil is a key input for transport, manufacturing, plastics, chemicals and agriculture, and its price feeds into the costs of almost every firm. A large fall in global oil prices therefore reduces costs of production across the UK economy.

Because input costs fall, firms can produce each level of output more cheaply, so they are willing to supply more at every price level. Short-run aggregate supply shifts to the right, from SRAS1 to SRAS2. This is a shift rather than a movement along SRAS because it is caused by a change in costs, not by a change in the price level. The new equilibrium moves from E1 to E2: the price level falls from P1 to P2 and real output rises from Y1 to Y2. In practice this means lower inflation rather than a falling price level: petrol and diesel prices fall directly, and lower transport and energy costs feed through to food and other goods. Higher real output requires more labour, so employment rises and unemployment falls. This combination of lower inflation and higher output is the reverse of stagflation and is sometimes called a positive supply shock.

There may also be effects on aggregate demand. Lower fuel prices raise households' real disposable income, increasing consumption, and firms' lower costs may raise profits and investment, shifting AD to the right. Lower inflation may allow the Bank of England to keep interest rates lower than otherwise. Together these reinforce the rise in real output.

However, the size of the effect depends on several factors. The UK still produces some oil and gas in the North Sea, so a lower oil price reduces profits, investment and tax revenues in that sector, which partly offsets the gains. The effect also depends on how much of the price fall is passed on: retailers and refiners may not cut prices fully, and in the UK fuel duty and VAT make up a large share of the pump price, so a fall in crude prices causes a smaller percentage fall in petrol prices. Finally, if the fall in oil prices is due to a global recession, falling world demand for UK exports would shift AD left, and the overall effect on UK output could be negative. When oil prices fell sharply in 2014 to 2016 for supply reasons, UK inflation fell close to zero while growth continued, suggesting the benefits are significant when the fall is supply-driven.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: correct identification of oil as a cost that shifts SRAS, distinguished from a movement. Application: UK-specific features (North Sea, fuel duty, 2014 to 2016 episode). Analysis: full diagram-based chain from costs to SRAS, price level, output and employment, plus AD effects. Evaluation: the North Sea offset, pass-through, the cause of the price fall and historical evidence, giving a balanced, supported answer worthy of the top level for 10 marks.

check.q: Which of the following would cause a movement along the SRAS curve rather than a shift?
options: Rise in the price of imported raw materials
Rise in the price level caused by an increase in AD
Increase in employer National Insurance contributions
Fall in global energy prices
check.explanation: A change in the price level, caused by a shift in AD, moves the economy along SRAS. The other options change costs and shift SRAS.

check.q: Why does the SRAS curve slope upwards?
options: Because consumers buy more when prices fall
Because some input costs are fixed in the short run, so a higher price level raises profitability
Because productive capacity rises when prices rise
Because the government increases spending when prices rise
check.explanation: With money wages and other costs fixed, a higher price level widens profit margins, and firms expand output, though at rising marginal cost.

check.q: In the classical model, what is the long-run effect of a permanent increase in AD when the economy starts at full employment?
options: Higher output and a higher price level
Higher output and the same price level
The same output and a higher price level
Lower output and a higher price level
check.explanation: In the short run output rises above Yfe, but as money wages adjust SRAS shifts left until output returns to Yfe at a higher price level.

check.q: Which of the following would shift LRAS to the right?
options: Fall in the price of oil
Cut in VAT
Improvement in the skills of the workforce
Rise in consumer confidence
check.explanation: Better skills increase the quality of labour and the productive capacity of the economy. A and B shift SRAS; D shifts AD.

title: Short-run AS
overview: Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) shifts when firms' costs of production change. The specification identifies three key influences: changes in the costs of raw materials and energy, changes in exchange rates, and changes in tax rates; wage costs and productivity are also central. Supply shocks explain episodes such as the 1970s oil crises and the UK's 2022 inflation surge, and they create a dilemma for policy makers because they push inflation and output in opposite directions. This topic gives you the tools to analyse cost shocks precisely and evaluate their impact.
objectives: Explain why changes in costs of production shift the SRAS curve.
Analyse the effects of changes in raw material and energy costs, exchange rates and taxes on SRAS.
Calculate changes in unit labour costs and import costs and explain their effect on SRAS.
Analyse the effects of SRAS shifts on the price level, real output and employment using AD/AS diagrams.
Evaluate the significance of supply shocks, including persistence, second-round effects and the policy dilemma they create.

sections.heading: Why cost changes shift SRAS
sections.body:
The SRAS curve is drawn on the assumption that input costs, especially money wages and raw material prices, are given. When those costs change, firms are willing to supply a different quantity of output at every price level, so the whole curve shifts.
- **Higher costs** reduce profit margins at every price level. Firms supply less at each price level, or need a higher price to supply the same output: SRAS shifts **left** (upwards).
- **Lower costs** raise margins, so firms supply more at each price level: SRAS shifts **right** (downwards).

An SRAS shift is different from an LRAS shift. SRAS shifts reflect changes in the cost of using existing capacity; they do not change how much the economy could produce if all resources were fully employed. A rise in energy prices makes production more expensive but does not destroy factories or workers' skills. (If a cost shock is very persistent, however, it can reduce potential output, for example by making energy-intensive industries permanently unviable.)

The effects of a leftward SRAS shift, with AD unchanged:
- The price level rises (cost-push inflation).
- Real output falls, so employment falls and unemployment rises.
- The combination is **stagflation**.

The effects of a rightward SRAS shift are the reverse: lower inflation, higher output and employment. This is why falling commodity prices or productivity improvements are described as **positive supply shocks**.

The main causes of SRAS shifts, examined in the following sections, are costs of raw materials and energy, exchange rates, taxes and subsidies, and wage costs relative to productivity.

sections.heading: Raw materials and energy
sections.body:
Raw materials (metals, timber, agricultural commodities) and energy (oil, gas, electricity) are inputs into almost all production. Their prices are set largely in **world markets**, so the UK is a price taker, and they can be very volatile because both demand and supply are price inelastic in the short run.

**Energy is the most important cost shock** because it affects every stage of production and distribution: manufacturing, heating premises, transport and food production (fertiliser production uses large amounts of natural gas). When energy prices rise:
- Energy-intensive industries such as steel, chemicals, ceramics and glass face sharp cost increases; some cut production or close.
- Transport costs rise, raising the price of almost all goods.
- Food prices rise as fertiliser, processing and refrigeration costs increase.

**UK example.** After Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, European wholesale gas prices rose several-fold. The UK depends heavily on gas for heating and electricity generation, so costs rose throughout the economy. SRAS shifted left: CPI inflation reached 11.1% in October 2022 while real GDP stagnated. The government's Energy Price Guarantee and Energy Bill Relief Scheme for businesses limited the cost increase, preventing a larger leftward shift.

**Historical example.** The oil price shocks of 1973 to 1974 and 1979, when oil prices roughly quadrupled and then more than doubled, caused stagflation across advanced economies, with UK inflation exceeding 20% in 1975.

**Positive shocks** occur when commodity prices fall. Oil prices fell by more than half between mid-2014 and early 2016, shifting SRAS right in oil-importing countries and helping to push UK inflation close to zero in 2015.

The size of the SRAS shift depends on the **share of the input in total costs** and on whether firms can **substitute** cheaper alternatives, for example switching to renewable energy or improving energy efficiency, which is more feasible in the long run than in the short run.

sections.heading: Exchange rates
sections.body:
The exchange rate affects SRAS through the **cost of imported inputs**. The UK imports a large share of its raw materials, energy, components and machinery, many priced in US dollars.
- A **depreciation** of sterling raises the sterling price of imports. If oil is $80 a barrel, it costs £61.54 at £1 = $1.30 but £66.67 at £1 = $1.20, an 8.3% increase even though the dollar price is unchanged. Higher input costs shift SRAS **left**.
- An **appreciation** lowers import costs and shifts SRAS **right**.

This is an important complication when analysing exchange rate changes. A depreciation increases AD (by raising net exports) and reduces SRAS (by raising import costs). Both effects raise the price level, so a depreciation is clearly inflationary, but the effects on real output work in opposite directions. The net effect on output depends on the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports and on how import-intensive UK production is.

**UK example.** After the June 2016 EU referendum, sterling fell sharply against both the dollar and the euro. Import prices rose over the following year, and CPI inflation increased from around 0.5% in mid-2016 to around 3% by late 2017. Real wages fell as a result, a cost of the depreciation that offset the competitive gain for exporters.

The impact depends on **pass-through**: how much of the change in import costs is passed on to final prices. Firms may absorb part of the cost by accepting lower margins, particularly in competitive markets, and many firms **hedge** currency risk using forward contracts, which delays the effect by months. Pass-through also tends to be larger when demand is strong and smaller when firms fear losing customers.

sections.heading: Taxes, subsidies and regulation
sections.body:
**Indirect taxes**, such as VAT, excise duties on fuel, alcohol and tobacco, and environmental levies, are paid by firms and raise the cost of supplying goods. An increase shifts SRAS left and raises the price level directly. The rise in VAT from 17.5% to 20% in January 2011 temporarily added to UK CPI inflation, which reached over 5% in late 2011.

**Taxes on employment** raise labour costs. Employer National Insurance contributions (NICs) are a tax on firms for each worker employed above a threshold. In April 2025 the UK raised the main rate of employer NICs from 13.8% to 15% and cut the threshold at which firms start paying from £9,100 to £5,000 a year, a large increase in the cost of employing staff, particularly part-time and low-paid workers. This shifts SRAS left.

**Business rates and corporation tax** also affect costs, though corporation tax is a tax on profits rather than on production, so it has a smaller direct effect on SRAS and a bigger effect on investment and LRAS.

**Subsidies** reduce costs and shift SRAS right. For example, the Energy Bill Relief Scheme in 2022 to 2023 limited energy costs for businesses, and fuel duty has been frozen in cash terms since 2011, with a temporary 5p cut from 2022, which reduces transport costs relative to what they would otherwise be.

**Regulation** can raise compliance costs: new environmental standards, health and safety rules, carbon pricing such as the UK Emissions Trading Scheme, or packaging rules all add to costs. These may be justified by the external costs they address (a link to market failure in 1.3), but in the short run they shift SRAS left.

sections.heading: Wages, productivity and unit labour costs
sections.body:
Labour is the largest cost for most firms, accounting for roughly half or more of total costs across the economy. But what matters for SRAS is not the wage rate alone; it is the labour cost **per unit of output**, called **unit labour cost (ULC)**:

ULC = total labour costs / total output

If wages rise at the same rate as productivity (output per worker), ULC is unchanged and SRAS does not shift. If wages rise faster than productivity, ULC rises and SRAS shifts left.

**Worked example.** A firm employs 50 workers at £600 a week (total labour cost £30,000) and produces 6,000 units: ULC = £5. Next year wages rise 6% to £636 (total £31,800) and output per worker rises 1% (output 6,060): ULC = 31,800 / 6,060 = £5.25, a rise of 5.0%. As a rule of thumb, % change in ULC ≈ % change in wages - % change in productivity = 6% - 1% = 5%.

This is why the UK's weak productivity growth since 2008 matters for inflation: with productivity growing only slowly, even moderate wage growth raises unit labour costs. In 2023 to 2024, UK nominal wage growth of around 6 to 8% far exceeded productivity growth, which is why the Bank of England watched wage growth and services inflation closely.

**Minimum wages** raise the cost of low-paid labour. The National Living Wage rose by 9.8% to £11.44 in April 2024 and by 6.7% to £12.21 in April 2025. Sectors with many low-paid workers, such as hospitality, retail and social care, face the largest cost increases.

**Short-run productivity changes** can also shift SRAS: better management, improved organisation or the use of existing technology more efficiently reduce costs per unit. Strictly, lasting productivity growth shifts LRAS too, which is covered in 2.3.3.

sections.heading: Evaluating supply shocks
sections.body:
When analysing an SRAS shift, the key evaluation questions are:
- **Size**: how large is the cost increase, and what share of total costs does the input represent? Energy shocks matter more than changes in the price of a minor input.
- **Duration**: is the shock temporary or persistent? A one-off rise in the price level shows up as inflation for a year and then drops out (a **base effect**). Inflation persists only if the shock continues or causes **second-round effects**.
- **Second-round effects**: if workers respond to higher prices by demanding higher wages to protect their real incomes, firms' costs rise again, shifting SRAS left once more: a **wage-price spiral**. This is more likely when the labour market is tight and when inflation expectations are not well anchored.
- **Pass-through**: firms may absorb some of the cost increase in lower profit margins, especially when demand is weak or competition is intense, reducing the effect on prices but also reducing profits and investment.
- **Policy response**: a leftward SRAS shift creates a dilemma. Raising interest rates to curb inflation deepens the fall in output; cutting interest rates to support output adds to inflation. Central banks usually look through temporary supply shocks but act to prevent second-round effects, which is what the Bank of England tried to do in 2022 to 2023.
- **Simultaneous AD effects**: many cost changes also affect AD. Higher energy prices reduce real disposable incomes, shifting AD left too, which offsets some of the inflationary pressure but deepens the fall in output.

The ability of firms to adapt also matters: in the long run they can switch energy sources, automate or relocate, so the effects of a cost shock tend to be smaller in the long run than in the short run.

key_terms.definition: The costs firms incur in producing output, including wages, raw materials, energy, rent and taxes on production.
A sudden, unexpected change in costs of production that shifts SRAS, such as a sharp change in oil or gas prices.
The labour cost of producing one unit of output: total labour costs divided by total output.
Output per worker or per hour worked.
The extent to which a change in costs, such as import prices, is passed on to consumer prices.
Further increases in prices and wages that follow an initial cost shock as workers and firms try to protect their real incomes and margins.
The effect on the annual inflation rate of a large price change twelve months earlier dropping out of the comparison.
A tax on expenditure, such as VAT or excise duty, paid by firms and usually passed on in prices.
A UK tax paid by employers on employees' earnings above a threshold, which adds to the cost of employing labour.
A situation of rising inflation together with falling or stagnant output and rising unemployment.

diagrams.title: Energy price shock: SRAS shifts left
diagrams.caption: A rise in energy costs, higher import prices after a depreciation or a rise in employer NICs shifts SRAS from SRAS1 to SRAS2. The price level rises from P1 to P2 and real output falls from Y1 to Y2: stagflation.

diagrams.title: Falling input costs: SRAS shifts right
diagrams.caption: Lower commodity prices, an appreciation of sterling or a cut in indirect taxes shift SRAS right. The price level falls from P1 to P2 (in practice, inflation falls) and real output rises from Y1 to Y2.

formulae.name: Unit labour cost
formulae.formula: Total labour costs / total output

formulae.name: Approximate change in ULC
formulae.formula: % change in wages - % change in labour productivity
formulae.example: Wages +6%, productivity +1%: ULC rises by about 5%.

formulae.name: Sterling cost of an import
formulae.formula: Foreign currency price / exchange rate

applications: In 2022 European gas prices rose several-fold after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The UK's heavy reliance on gas for heating and power meant SRAS shifted sharply left: CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022 while output stagnated. Government energy support for households and businesses limited the shift.

From April 2025 employer NICs rose from 13.8% to 15% and the threshold fell from £9,100 to £5,000, while the National Living Wage rose 6.7% to £12.21. Retailers and hospitality firms warned of higher prices and fewer jobs, a clear case of rising labour costs shifting SRAS left.
The fall in sterling after the 2016 referendum raised import costs and pushed CPI inflation to around 3% by late 2017, demonstrating how exchange rate changes shift SRAS and erode real wages.

The oil shocks of the 1970s caused stagflation across advanced economies. UK inflation exceeded 20% in 1975, and the experience of a wage-price spiral shaped later policy, including central bank independence and inflation targeting.
evaluation: Persistence matters: a one-off cost shock raises the price level once, and inflation falls back as base effects come through; inflation only persists if there are second-round effects on wages and expectations.
The share of the input in total costs determines the size of the SRAS shift: energy and labour matter far more than minor inputs.
Pass-through is often incomplete: firms may absorb costs in lower margins or hedge currency risk, so the inflationary effect may be smaller and slower than a diagram suggests.
Many cost changes also shift AD (higher energy prices cut real incomes; a depreciation raises net exports), so the net effect on output and prices requires analysis of both curves.
Supply shocks create a policy dilemma: monetary tightening reduces inflation but deepens the fall in output, so the appropriate response depends on whether expectations are anchored.
Firms adapt in the long run through substitution, efficiency and innovation, so long-run effects are usually smaller than short-run effects.
misconceptions: Shifting LRAS for a temporary cost increase. Higher energy prices or taxes shift SRAS; they do not destroy productive capacity unless they are permanent and severe.
Assuming that higher wages always shift SRAS left. If productivity rises by the same amount, unit labour costs are unchanged.
Thinking a depreciation only affects AD. It also raises import costs and shifts SRAS left.
Drawing SRAS shifting downwards to show higher costs. Higher costs shift SRAS left (upwards); lower costs shift it right (downwards).
Treating a one-off rise in the price level as persistent inflation. Once the shock passes, annual inflation falls back unless there are second-round effects.
exam_tips: Always name the specific cost that changes and explain why it shifts SRAS (effect on costs per unit and profit margins at each price level).
Unit labour cost calculations may appear in Section A: compute total labour cost and output, or use the approximation wages minus productivity.
For 12 and 15-mark questions on a cost shock, evaluate with size, persistence, pass-through, second-round effects and the policy dilemma.
Use precise UK examples: 2022 energy shock, 2025 employer NICs and NLW rises, 2016 depreciation, 2011 VAT rise.
Synoptic links: cost-push inflation (2.1.2), labour markets and minimum wages (3.5.3), exchange rates (4.1.8) and indirect taxes (1.2.9).

model_answer.question: Assess the likely impact of the April 2025 increase in employer National Insurance contributions on short-run aggregate supply and the UK economy. (12 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Employer National Insurance contributions are a tax paid by employers on employees' earnings above a threshold. In April 2025 the main rate rose from 13.8% to 15% and the threshold fell from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. Short-run aggregate supply is the total output firms will supply at each price level when input costs are given.

The increase raises the cost of employing labour. For a worker earning £25,000 a year, the employer's NICs bill rises from around £2,195 to £3,000, an increase of over a third. Because labour is the largest cost for most firms, unit labour costs rise. At every price level firms' profit margins are lower, so they are willing to supply less output: SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2. The price level rises from P1 to P2 (cost-push inflation) and real output falls from Y1 to Y2. With lower output, firms need fewer workers, so employment may fall. The lower threshold means the increase is proportionately largest for part-time and low-paid workers, so labour-intensive sectors such as hospitality, retail and social care are most affected. These firms also faced a 6.7% rise in the National Living Wage to £12.21 at the same time, compounding the cost increase.

However, the size of the SRAS shift may be smaller than this suggests. Smaller firms were partly protected because the Employment Allowance, which reduces their NICs bill, rose from £5,000 to £10,500, so many small employers pay little or nothing extra. More importantly, the incidence of the tax may fall largely on workers rather than firms. Over time, firms may respond by offering lower pay rises than they otherwise would, so the cost is shared with workers through slower wage growth; the OBR expected most of the cost to be passed on to workers in this way within a few years. If wages adjust, the long-run increase in unit labour costs, and hence the shift in SRAS, is reduced, although real incomes and consumption are lower, shifting AD left.

The effect also depends on firms' ability to pass costs on. In markets where demand is weak and competition intense, firms may absorb the cost in lower profits rather than raising prices, limiting inflation but reducing investment. Where they can pass it on, prices rise; business surveys in 2025 suggested many retailers and hospitality firms planned to raise prices and reduce hiring.

Overall, the increase in employer NICs is likely to have shifted SRAS left modestly, raising prices and reducing employment in labour-intensive, low-margin sectors in the short run. The aggregate effect is limited by the Employment Allowance and by the gradual passing of costs to workers through lower wage growth, but this means the burden shifts from firms to workers rather than disappearing, so the policy also reduces real incomes and AD.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate description of the policy and of SRAS. Application: precise rates and thresholds, a numerical illustration, the NLW rise and the Employment Allowance. Analysis: a clear chain from labour costs to unit labour costs, SRAS, prices, output and employment, with sectoral detail. Evaluation: considers incidence (shifting to wages over time), pass-through and protection for small firms, and reaches a balanced judgement about who bears the cost, meeting Level 3.

title: Long-run AS
overview: Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) represents the productive capacity of the economy, and its growth determines long-run living standards. This topic covers the two competing views of LRAS, the classical (vertical) and Keynesian (horizontal, then curving, then vertical) curves, and the factors that shift LRAS: technology, productivity, education and skills, government regulation, demographic change and migration, and competition policy. The classical vs Keynesian debate underpins almost every policy evaluation in Theme 2, and the UK's productivity puzzle makes this one of the most relevant topics for essays.
objectives: Explain and draw the classical and Keynesian LRAS curves and the assumptions behind each.
Analyse how an increase in AD affects output and prices under each view of LRAS.
Explain how technology, productivity, education and skills, regulation, demographics and migration, and competition policy shift LRAS.
Analyse the effects of a rightward shift of LRAS on output, the price level and employment.
Evaluate which factors are most important for raising UK productive capacity and how quickly they work.

sections.heading: The classical LRAS
sections.body:
In the **classical (free-market, monetarist)** view, LRAS is **vertical** at the full-employment level of output, **Yfe**, also called potential output or the natural level of output.

The reasoning rests on **flexible prices and wages**. In the long run, if the price level rises, workers demand and obtain proportionately higher money wages, and other input prices also rise. Real wages and the real profitability of production are unchanged, so firms have no incentive to supply more. Output in the long run therefore depends only on the **quantity and quality of factors of production** and the **technology** with which they are combined, not on the price level.

Key implications:
- **Markets self-correct.** If output falls below Yfe, unemployment puts downward pressure on wages and prices, SRAS shifts right and the economy returns to full employment without government intervention.
- **Demand-side policy is ineffective in the long run.** An increase in AD from AD1 to AD2 raises output above Yfe only temporarily; as wages adjust, the economy returns to Yfe at a higher price level (see diagram and the adjustment diagram in 2.3.1). The long-run result is inflation only.
- **Supply-side policy is the route to growth.** The only way to raise output sustainably is to shift LRAS to the right by increasing productive capacity.

Full employment does not mean zero unemployment: at Yfe there is still frictional and structural unemployment, the **natural rate of unemployment**. Classical economists argue that the natural rate can be reduced only by supply-side measures, such as better job matching, training and incentives to work.

sections.heading: The Keynesian LRAS
sections.body:
Keynes and his followers argued that the economy can remain below full employment for long periods because **wages are sticky downwards**: workers resist money wage cuts, contracts fix pay, and firms fear damaging morale. If wages and prices do not fall, the economy does not self-correct, and there can be a long-lasting **negative output gap**.

The **Keynesian LRAS** curve has three ranges (see diagram):
- **Horizontal range**: with a large amount of spare capacity (mass unemployment and idle capital), firms can expand output without bidding up costs. An increase in AD raises real output with no rise in the price level.
- **Intermediate (curved) range**: as output rises, **bottlenecks** appear. Some industries and regions reach capacity before others, some skills become scarce and firms bid up wages and input prices. An increase in AD raises both output and the price level.
- **Vertical range**: at full capacity (Yfe) all resources are employed. Any further increase in AD only raises the price level.

Key implications:
- **Demand-side policy can be very effective** when there is spare capacity. Keynesians argue governments should use fiscal policy to raise AD in a recession, as in 2009 and 2020.
- **Unemployment can persist** because of insufficient AD, not just supply-side problems.
- **Hysteresis**: a long recession can reduce future capacity as workers lose skills and firms cut investment, so failing to support AD can shift LRAS left.

The two views agree that there is a maximum level of output (the vertical section) and that supply-side improvements shift it outwards. They disagree about whether the economy is normally near that maximum and how quickly it returns there after a shock. In practice, many economists take a middle position: classical analysis applies in the long run, but the short run can last a long time, especially after a deep recession.

sections.heading: Technology and productivity
sections.body:
**Productivity** is output per unit of input, most commonly **labour productivity**: output per worker or per hour worked. Higher productivity means the same resources produce more, shifting LRAS right. It is the single most important determinant of long-run living standards.

**Technology** raises productivity by allowing more output from the same inputs. Examples include automation and robotics in manufacturing, cloud computing and data analytics in services, and artificial intelligence, which could raise productivity in professional and administrative work. New technology usually enters the economy through **investment** in new capital and through **research and development (R&D)**. It also creates entirely new products and industries.

Other sources of productivity growth:
- **Capital deepening**: giving workers more and better capital (machines, software).
- **Better management and organisation**: UK evidence suggests a long tail of poorly managed, low-productivity firms.
- **Reallocation**: resources moving from low-productivity firms and sectors to high-productivity ones, which depends on competition and flexible markets.
- **Infrastructure**: reliable transport, energy and digital networks reduce costs and widen markets.

**The UK productivity puzzle.** Before the 2008 financial crisis, UK labour productivity grew by around 2% a year. Since then it has grown by only around 0.5% a year on average, and UK output per hour is below that of the USA, Germany and France. Explanations include low business and public investment, weak diffusion of technology to smaller firms, a long tail of low-productivity firms, the after-effects of the financial crisis on credit and risk-taking, uncertainty after 2016, and planning constraints on infrastructure and housing. Had pre-crisis productivity growth continued, UK GDP per head would be far higher today, which shows how much LRAS growth matters.

sections.heading: Education, skills and the labour force
sections.body:
**Education and skills** raise the quality of labour, known as **human capital**. Better-educated workers are more productive, adapt more easily to new technology, and are more likely to innovate. They also reduce **occupational immobility**, lowering structural unemployment. Education and training therefore shift LRAS to the right.

UK policy examples include the apprenticeship levy (introduced in 2017), T-levels, reforms to adult skills funding, and university and further education expansion. Concerns remain: apprenticeship starts fell significantly after the levy was introduced, and international surveys show the UK has a relatively large number of adults with low basic literacy and numeracy. Improving early years and school education has a large long-run payoff, but it takes **decades** to affect the workforce, so its effect on LRAS is slow.

**Demographic changes and migration** affect the **quantity** of labour:
- An **ageing population** reduces the share of people of working age, slowing labour force growth and potentially shifting LRAS left relative to trend, while raising demand for health and care.
- **Net inward migration** increases the labour force. Most migrants are of working age, and many fill skill shortages in health, care and engineering, shifting LRAS right. Net migration of roughly 900,000 in the year to mid-2023 significantly increased the UK labour force.
- **Participation**: the share of the working-age population in work or seeking work. Rising economic inactivity due to long-term sickness, which reached around 2.8 million people in 2024, reduced UK labour supply after the pandemic. Policies on health, childcare and incentives to work can raise participation and shift LRAS right.

Note the distinction between total LRAS and LRAS per head: migration raises total productive capacity, but living standards depend on output per head, which requires productivity growth.

sections.heading: Regulation and competition policy
sections.body:
**Government regulations** affect LRAS in both directions:
- **Excessive or poorly designed regulation** raises costs, discourages investment and slows the adoption of new technology. The UK planning system is often cited: long delays in approving housing, wind farms, grid connections and transport infrastructure hold back investment and labour mobility. Reducing unnecessary red tape (deregulation) can shift LRAS right.
- **Well-designed regulation** can raise LRAS by correcting market failures: protecting property rights and intellectual property encourages innovation; financial regulation reduces the risk of crises that damage capacity; health and safety rules protect workers' long-term productivity.

**Competition policy** promotes competition by preventing anti-competitive mergers, abuse of market power and cartels. In the UK this is the role of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). Competition shifts LRAS right because:
- Firms facing competition have stronger incentives to cut costs (productive efficiency) and innovate (dynamic efficiency).
- Less efficient firms lose market share to more efficient ones, reallocating resources to their most productive uses.
- Lower barriers to entry allow new, innovative firms to grow.

Other supply-side influences on LRAS, covered in 2.6.3, include tax incentives for investment and work, labour market reforms, infrastructure spending and privatisation. Institutional factors such as the rule of law, political stability and well-functioning financial markets are also important, particularly for developing economies (4.3.2).

**Effects of a rightward shift of LRAS.** With AD unchanged, an increase in LRAS from LRAS1 to LRAS2 raises real output and lowers the price level (see diagram). In a growing economy, LRAS shifting right at the same pace as AD allows **non-inflationary growth**, improves international competitiveness and can raise employment. This is why supply-side improvements are seen as the key to sustained growth.

sections.heading: Evaluating LRAS growth
sections.body:
When evaluating any factor or policy that shifts LRAS, consider:
- **Time lags.** Education reforms take decades to affect the workforce; infrastructure takes years to plan and build; R&D may take years to yield products. Technology adoption is faster but still gradual. Shifts in LRAS are therefore slow and uncertain.
- **Magnitude.** Some factors have a much larger effect than others. Productivity growth is the dominant driver of long-run growth in output per head; labour force growth raises total output but not necessarily output per person.
- **Interaction with AD.** If LRAS shifts right but AD does not grow, the result may be falling prices and unused capacity rather than higher output. Supply and demand-side policies are complementary.
- **Distribution.** Technological change can increase inequality by raising demand for high-skilled workers while displacing routine jobs, creating structural unemployment in some regions.
- **Costs and opportunity cost.** Supply-side spending on education or infrastructure must be financed, with an opportunity cost elsewhere; deregulation may have environmental or social costs.
- **Measurement.** Potential output cannot be observed directly; estimates by the OBR and the Bank of England are uncertain and frequently revised.
- **Which LRAS view applies.** If the economy is in the horizontal range of the Keynesian curve, raising capacity without raising AD adds little to output in the short run.

Strong essays use these angles to rank factors and conclude, for example, that for the UK raising investment and technology diffusion probably offers the largest medium-term gains, education the largest long-run gains, and migration the fastest increase in total, but not per capita, capacity.

key_terms.definition: The productive capacity of the economy: the total output that can be produced when all resources are fully and efficiently employed.
A vertical LRAS curve at the full-employment level of output, reflecting the view that prices and wages are flexible in the long run.
An AS curve that is horizontal when there is spare capacity, curves upwards as bottlenecks appear and becomes vertical at full capacity.
Output per unit of input, most often output per worker or per hour worked.
The skills, knowledge, education and health of the workforce that determine its productivity.
The knowledge and techniques used to combine factors of production, including new machinery, processes and products.
Shortages of particular resources, skills or capacity in some sectors that cause costs and prices to rise before the economy as a whole reaches full capacity.
The rate of unemployment at full-employment output, consisting of frictional and structural unemployment.
Government policy to promote competition and prevent anti-competitive behaviour, enforced in the UK by the CMA.
The unusually slow growth of UK labour productivity since the 2008 financial crisis compared with previous decades and other countries.
The effect by which a prolonged recession reduces future productive capacity, for example through lost skills and investment.
Growth in real output without rising inflation, possible when LRAS shifts right in line with AD.

diagrams.title: Classical LRAS: higher AD only raises prices
diagrams.caption: With a vertical classical LRAS, an increase in AD from AD1 to AD2 leaves real output at Yfe in the long run and raises the price level from P1 to P2.

diagrams.title: Classical LRAS shifts right
diagrams.caption: Better technology, skills, investment or a larger labour force shift LRAS from LRAS1 to LRAS2. Real output rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from P1 to P2, allowing non-inflationary growth.

diagrams.title: The Keynesian AS curve
diagrams.caption: In the horizontal range (AD1) higher AD raises output with no inflation; in the intermediate range (AD2) bottlenecks mean both output and prices rise; in the vertical range (AD3) higher AD only raises the price level.

diagrams.title: Keynesian LRAS shifts right
diagrams.caption: Supply-side improvements extend full-capacity output, shifting the Keynesian LRAS right. With AD near capacity, output rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from P1 to P2. If AD were in the horizontal range, the shift would have little effect on output.

formulae.name: Labour productivity
formulae.formula: Total output / number of workers (or hours worked)

formulae.name: Growth in output
formulae.formula: % change in output ≈ % change in labour input + % change in labour productivity

applications: UK labour productivity grew by around 2% a year before 2008 but only around 0.5% a year since. This productivity puzzle means LRAS has shifted right far more slowly than in previous decades, and it is the main reason why UK real wages and GDP per head have grown so slowly.

Net migration of roughly 900,000 in the year to mid-2023 increased the UK labour force and total productive capacity, but rising inactivity due to long-term sickness, at around 2.8 million people in 2024, worked in the opposite direction, illustrating how demographic and health factors shift LRAS.

UK governments have pursued supply-side measures including full expensing for investment, the apprenticeship levy, planning reform to speed up housing and infrastructure, and the National Wealth Fund. Their success depends on how far they raise investment and productivity rather than just total output.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence could raise productivity in services, which make up around 80% of UK output. Estimates of its effect vary widely, and the gains depend on adoption by firms and on workers having the skills to use it.

South Korea and Singapore raised productive capacity rapidly through heavy investment in education, technology and infrastructure, showing how sustained supply-side improvement can transform LRAS over a few decades.
evaluation: The classical and Keynesian views disagree about how quickly the economy self-corrects; the answer probably depends on the size of the shock and wage flexibility, so neither view is right in all circumstances.
Time lags vary greatly: migration raises labour supply quickly, investment and technology take years, and education reforms take decades.
Total vs per capita: a larger labour force raises LRAS but not necessarily output per head; living standards depend mainly on productivity growth.
Supply-side improvements raise output only if AD is sufficient to use the new capacity; in a recession, demand-side support may be needed alongside.
Distributional effects matter: technological change may raise average productivity while displacing workers and widening regional inequality.
Estimates of potential output are uncertain and revised, so policy makers cannot be sure how far the economy is from LRAS at any time.
misconceptions: Drawing the classical LRAS as upward sloping. It is vertical at Yfe because in the long run output is independent of the price level.
Saying that AD has no effect on output in any circumstances. Even classical economists accept that AD affects output in the short run; Keynesians argue the short run can be very long.
Treating higher energy prices or tax changes as LRAS shifts. Cost changes shift SRAS; LRAS shifts when the quantity or quality of resources or technology changes.
Assuming migration automatically raises living standards. It raises total capacity, but output per head depends on productivity.
Thinking supply-side policies work quickly. Most take years, so they cannot fix a recession.
exam_tips: Learn to draw both LRAS curves accurately and label the three Keynesian ranges. Many Paper 2 essays reward using the Keynesian curve to evaluate demand-side policy.
When asked about a factor shifting LRAS, state whether it changes the quantity or quality of factors or technology, then explain the effect on productivity and productive capacity.
In 25-mark essays, rank the factors using time lags, magnitude, cost and evidence, and distinguish total output from output per head.
Use UK productivity data and specific policies (apprenticeship levy, full expensing, planning reform, migration rules) to gain application marks.
Synoptic links: supply-side policies (2.6.3), economic growth and output gaps (2.5.1, 2.5.2), development (4.3.2) and efficiency and competition (3.4.1, 3.6.1).

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that improving education and skills is the most effective way to increase long-run aggregate supply in the UK. (25 marks)
model_answer.answer:
Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) represents the productive capacity of the economy: the output that can be produced when all resources are fully and efficiently employed. It depends on the quantity and quality of factors of production and on technology. Education and skills improve the quality of labour, known as human capital.

Improving education and skills raises labour productivity: better-educated workers produce more per hour, make fewer errors, and can use more advanced capital. For example, workers trained in data analysis or engineering can use automation and AI to raise output, whereas workers without these skills cannot. Higher productivity means the same labour force produces more, so LRAS shifts right from LRAS1 to LRAS2. With AD unchanged, real output rises and the price level falls, allowing non-inflationary growth. Education also reduces occupational immobility: workers with transferable skills can move from declining industries to growing ones, reducing structural unemployment and so bringing more of the labour force into productive use. In addition, education supports innovation: a well-educated workforce is more likely to develop new products and processes, raising dynamic efficiency. Since growth in output per head ultimately depends on productivity, and the UK's productivity growth has slowed from around 2% a year before 2008 to around 0.5% since, improving skills addresses the central weakness of the UK economy.

There is specific evidence that skills are a constraint in the UK. International surveys show the UK has a relatively large number of adults with low literacy and numeracy, and employers regularly report skill shortages in engineering, construction and digital roles. Apprenticeship starts fell significantly after the apprenticeship levy was introduced in 2017, suggesting the training system is not delivering enough technical skills. Countries with strong technical education systems, such as Germany, have higher productivity in manufacturing.

However, there are reasons to doubt that education and skills are the most effective route. First, time lags are very long. Reforms to early years and school education take ten to twenty years to affect the workforce, and even adult training takes years to reach large numbers. Other factors can shift LRAS much more quickly. Second, skills raise productivity only if they are combined with sufficient capital and technology. UK business investment has been around 10% of GDP, among the lowest in the G7. A skilled worker without modern equipment is less productive than a less skilled worker with it. This suggests that low investment, rather than low skills, may be the binding constraint. Policies such as full expensing, which lets firms deduct investment from taxable profits immediately, may have a faster and larger effect on productivity. Third, the UK already has a high proportion of graduates by international standards, yet productivity growth has been weak; some graduates work in jobs that do not use their degrees (underemployment), suggesting that more education alone does not raise productivity unless the economy creates high-skill jobs.

Other factors may also be more effective in specific circumstances. Raising labour force participation by tackling long-term sickness, which affected around 2.8 million inactive people in 2024, could increase the quantity of labour quickly. Migration can raise LRAS almost immediately by filling skill shortages, though it raises total output more than output per head. Planning reform could unlock investment in housing, energy and transport infrastructure that has been held back for years, reducing costs and improving labour mobility. Competition policy, by forcing less efficient firms to improve or exit, can raise average productivity.

The effectiveness of education also depends on its quality and focus. Spending on early years and basic skills has high long-run returns, while poorly designed training schemes may have low returns. There is also an opportunity cost: public spending on education must be financed by taxes or borrowing, which may limit other supply-side investment.

In conclusion, improving education and skills is essential for sustained increases in LRAS, because productivity growth is the main source of rising output per head and human capital determines how well new technology is used. However, it is unlikely to be the most effective single policy for the UK in the short to medium term, because of long time lags and because the binding constraint appears to be low investment and slow technology adoption rather than a lack of graduates. The most effective approach combines skills policy, particularly technical and adult skills where the UK is weakest, with measures to raise business investment and reform planning, since skills and capital are complements: each raises the return to the other. Education is therefore the most important foundation in the long run, but not the fastest or most effective lever on its own.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of LRAS and human capital, with the LRAS diagram referenced. Application: UK productivity data, adult skills, apprenticeship levy, investment share, inactivity and policies such as full expensing and planning reform. Analysis: well-developed chains from skills to productivity, mobility and innovation. Evaluation: time lags, complementarity with capital, graduate underemployment, comparison with alternative factors and opportunity cost, reaching a nuanced judgement distinguishing short and long run. This meets Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.
